web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Syllabus Overview
web_content_rtb__content.value:
Organisation of Mathematics K–10

The syllabus structure illustrates the important role Working mathematically plays across all areas of mathematics and reflects the strengthened connections between concepts. Working mathematically has been embedded in the outcomes, content and examples of the syllabus.

Mathematics K–10 outcomes and their related content are organised in:

  • Number and algebra
  • Measurement and space
  • Statistics and probability
Working mathematically

The Working mathematically processes present in the Mathematics K–10 syllabus are:

  • communicating
  • understanding and fluency
  • reasoning
  • problem solving.

Students learn to work mathematically by using these processes in an interconnected way. The coordinated development of these processes results in students becoming mathematically proficient.

When students are Working mathematically it is important to help them to reflect on how they have used their thinking to solve problems. This assists students to develop ‘mathematical habits of mind’ (Cuoco et al. 2010).

Students need many experiences that require them to relate their knowledge to the vocabulary and conceptual frameworks of mathematics.

Overarching Working mathematically outcome

To highlight how these processes are interrelated, in Mathematics K–10 there is one overarching Working mathematically outcome.

A student develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through:

  • exploring and connecting mathematical concepts
  • choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems
  • communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly.

The Working mathematically outcome describes the thinking and doing of mathematics. In doing so, the outcome indicates the breadth of mathematical actions that teachers need to emphasise. The overarching Working mathematically outcome is the same across the K–10 Mathematics syllabus.

The Working mathematically processes should be embedded within the concepts being taught. Embedding Working mathematically ensures students are able to fluently understand concepts and make connections to other focus areas. The mathematics focus area outcomes and content provide the knowledge and skills for students to reason about, and contexts for problem solving. The overarching Working mathematically outcome is assessed in conjunction with the mathematics content outcomes. The sophistication of Working mathematically processes develops through each stage of learning and can be observed in relation to the increase in complexity of the mathematics outcomes and content. A student's level of competence in Working mathematically can be monitored over time, for example, within Additive Relations by the choice of strategy appropriate to the task, and the use of efficient strategy for the stage of learning the student is working at.

Further information is available in Elaborating on Working mathematically in K–10 (Word, 5 pages, 914.28 KB).

Image long description: An overview of the syllabus structure for Early Stage 1 and Stage 1 in Mathematics across the 3 areas of Number and algebra, Measurement and space, and Statistics and probability. Number and algebra reads horizontally across Representing whole numbers, Combining and separating quantities, and Forming groups. Measurement and space reads horizontally across Geometric measure, 2D spatial structure, 3D spatial structure, and Non-spatial measure. Statistics and probability reads horizontally across Data and Chance.

Image long description: An overview of the syllabus structure for Stages 2 and 3 in Mathematics across the 3 areas of Number and algebra, Measurement and space, and Statistics and probability. Number and algebra reads horizontally across 2 stages – Stage 2 and Stage 3. Stage 2 learning areas include Representing numbers using place value, Additive relations, Multiplicative relations and Partitioned fractions. Stage 3 learning areas include Represents numbers, Additive relations, Multiplicative relations, and Representing quality fractions. Measurement and space reads horizontally across 2 stages – Stages 2 and 3. Learning areas include Geometric measure, 2D spatial structure, 3D spatial structure, and Non-spatial measure. Statistics and probability reads horizontally across 2 stages – Stages 2 and 3. Learning areas include Data and Chance.

K–6 Parts A and B

Across a stage of learning all focus areas need to be taught. Mathematics focus areas outline the development of several concepts. In Mathematics K–6, where stages span 2 years of learning (for example, Stage 2 includes Year 3 and Year 4), there are concepts that may need to be addressed earlier or later in the stage.

To assist programming, the content in these focus areas has been separated into 2 parts, A and B, such as in Representing Numbers Using Place Value – A and Representing Numbers Using Place Value – B:

  • Part A typically focuses on early concept development
  • Part B builds on these early concepts.

The content across Parts A and B relates to the same stage-based outcomes. Teachers can choose which content from Part A and/or Part B to address, based on students’ prior learning, needs and abilities.

For example, in Stage 2, Part A does not equate to Year 3 only. When teaching a Year 4 class, the teacher may need to address or consolidate some concepts within Part A prior to addressing concepts in Part B. Similarly, when teaching a Year 3 class, the teacher may decide to address concepts in Part B based on the students’ prior learning, needs and abilities.

The Part A and Part B structure of the content:

  • provides flexibility for teachers in planning teaching and learning programs based on the needs and abilities of students
  • helps to better visualise the progression and growth of concepts within a stage of learning
  • makes clear how content builds to support deep understanding in each focus area.

Considerations for planning teaching and learning programs include:

  • when students may have learnt some concepts from Part B content in the first year of a stage, consolidation of these concepts in the second year of a stage may be needed
  • revisiting concepts regularly to build deeper understanding of mathematical concepts
  • providing extension of certain concepts based on students’ needs and abilities.

Access content points K–6

Image long description: Stage 4/5 Core: broad outcome groups are Number and finance, Algebra and equations, Ratios and rates, Linear and non-linear relationships, Pythagoras and trigonometry, Length, area and volume, Geometrical properties and figures, Data classification, visualisation and analysis and Probability. Stage 5 Paths: broad outcome groups are Further algebra and equations, Variation and rates of change, Functions and graphs, Further trigonometry, Further area and volume, Geometrical figures and proof, Introduction to networks, Data analysis and statistical enquiry and Further probability. All content is surrounded by the phrase, Working mathematically through communicating reasoning, understanding and fluency, and problem solving.

7–10 Core–Paths structure

The Core–Paths structure is designed to encourage aspiration in students. The structure is intended to extend students as far along the continuum of learning as possible and provide solid foundations for the highest levels of student achievement. The structure allows for a diverse range of endpoints up to the end of Stage 5.

Typically, the Core will cover teaching and learning experiences up to the middle of Stage 5. It is not the intention of the Core–Paths structure to lock students into predetermined pathways at the end of Stage 4.

Teachers program Path outcomes and content as appropriate to the needs of the students by the end of Stage 5. Paths may be implemented at any time in Stages 4 and 5.

The Core outcomes and content provide students with the foundation for Mathematics Standard 11–12.

Life Skills outcomes and content

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

Balance of content

The amount of content associated with a given outcome is not necessarily indicative of the amount of time spent engaging with the respective outcome. Teachers use formative and summative assessment to determine instructional priorities and the time needed for students to demonstrate expected outcomes.

In considering the intended learning, teachers make decisions about the sequence and emphasis to be given to particular groups of content based on the needs and abilities of their students.

Working at different stages

For example:

  • Students in Early Stage 1 could be working on Stage 1 content in the Number and Algebra strand, while working on Early Stage 1 content in the Measurement and Geometry strand.
  • In Stage 2 or Stage 3, some students may not have developed a complete understanding of place value and the role of zero to read, write and order two-digit and three-digit numbers. These students will need to access content from Early Stage 1 or Stage 1 before engaging with Stage 2 content in applying place value to larger numbers and decimals.
  • In Stage 4 some students may not have developed a complete understanding of fractions, decimals and percentages and will need to access related outcomes from Stage 3.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Courses 7–10

The Mathematics K–10 Syllabus includes 2 courses for Mathematics 7–10:

  • Mathematics
  • Mathematics Life Skills

Focus of learning

Students learn how to demonstrate understanding of the relationships between mathematical concepts. They develop skills in solving routine and non-routine problems and learn to use mathematical language to solve problems and communicate reasoning.

What students learn

Students develop knowledge, understanding and skills across Number and algebra, Measurement and space, and Statistics and probability.

Through the Core, students develop knowledge of number, finance, algebraic expressions and equations, ratios and rates, linear and non-linear relationships, trigonometry, geometry, data and multistage probability.

Through the Paths, students extend knowledge of the core through more complex content, including further algebraic techniques, graphing, geometrical proof, networks, statistical enquiry and further probability.

Course requirements

Teachers program all core outcomes and content as part of students’ curriculum entitlement.

Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the Mathematics K–10 Syllabus.

Life Skills

For Mathematics Life Skills:

  • Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Mathematics 7–10 Life Skills outcomes.
  • Outcomes and content should be selected to meet the particular needs of individual students.
  • The focus areas provide possible frameworks for addressing the Mathematics 7–10 Life Skills outcomes and content and are suggestions only. Teachers have the flexibility to select, group and sequence outcomes and content to meet the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students.
  • The Working mathematically processes provide an opportunity for students to develop knowledge and skills in communicating reasoning, understanding and fluency, and problem solving. There is one Working mathematically outcome for all courses, including Mathematics 7–10 Life Skills. Teachers should embed Working mathematically processes into teaching and learning activities where appropriate to the needs and abilities of students.

Students with disability can access the syllabus outcomes and content in a range of ways. Decisions regarding curriculum options should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Some students with intellectual disability may find the Years 7–10 Life Skills outcomes and content the most appropriate option to follow in Stage 4 and/or Stage 5. Teachers select specific Life Skills outcomes to teach based on the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of each student. Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Life Skills outcomes.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Manipulation of a variety of real objects and shapes is crucial to the development of appropriate levels of visualisation, language and representation. Also, measuring the areas of objects using informal units enables students to develop some key understandings of measurement. These include:

  • repeatedly placing units so that there are no gaps or overlaps
  • understanding that the units must be equal in size.

Teaching advice

2D shape

Representing and visualising three-dimensional objects and two-dimensional shapes are developing in Stage 1 and should be fostered through practical activities and communication.

Students should be able to recognise shapes presented in different orientations.

Students should have experiences identifying both regular shapes (all sides and angles equal) and irregular shapes. It is not expected that students understand or distinguish between regular and irregular shapes in Stage 1.

Area

Area relates to the measurement of two-dimensional space, in the same way that volume relates to the measurement of three-dimensional space. The attribute of area is the amount of surface (either flat or curved) and can be measured in square units:

  • square centimetres (cm2)
  • square metres (m2).

Informal units

Measuring the areas of objects using informal units enables students to develop some key understandings of measurement. These include:

  • repeatedly placing units so that there are no gaps or overlaps
  • understanding that the units must be equal in size.

Covering surfaces with a range of informal units should assist students in understanding that some units tessellate (fit together without gaps or overlaps) and are therefore more suitable for measuring area.

When students draw the covering of a rectangle with unit squares, some will draw each individual square while others will draw a combination of individual squares and lines. Some students will draw lines to represent rows and then mark off squares individually while others will draw an array using lines.

Grid structure

Students should be encouraged to make, draw and describe the spatial structure (grid) for rectangular shapes. To assist students in noticing the grid structure, outline cardboard square tiles.

Students should develop procedures for counting tile or grid units so that no units are missed or counted twice. They should be encouraged to identify and use efficient strategies for counting, eg using repeated addition or skip counting.

It is important that:

  • students have had some measurement experiences including cutting up and rearranging areas before being asked to estimate areas
  • a variety of estimation strategies is taught.

Language

2D shape

The term ‘vertex’ (plural: ‘vertices’) refers to the point where:

  • two straight sides of a two-dimensional shape meet
  • three or more faces of a three-dimensional object meet.

The term ‘shape’ refers to a two-dimensional figure. The term ‘object’ refers to a three-dimensional figure.

Students learn to identify a number of different polygons including:

  • triangles
  • quadrilaterals
  • pentagons
  • hexagons
  • octagons.

The names of these shapes reflect Latin and Greek influences:

  • Triangle: from the Latin triangulus, meaning three angles or corners. It is helpful to check if students know any other words where ‘tri’ also means three, such as tricycle or triceratops.
  • Quadrilateral: from the Latin quadrilaterus, meaning four sides or flanks. While squares and rectangles are examples of quadrilaterals, a square is also a special type of rectangle.
  • Polygon: comes from ancient Greek (written in the Latin alphabet) and means many angles. Pentagons (five angles), hexagons (six angles) and octagons (eight angles) are all examples of polygons.

A shape has line symmetry if matching parts are produced when it is folded along a line of symmetry. Each part represents the mirror image of the other.

Vocabulary

2D shape

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • shape
  • circle
  • triangle
  • quadrilateral
  • square
  • rectangle
  • pentagon
  • hexagon
  • octagon
  • orientation
  • features
  • side
  • vertex (vertices)
  • shape
  • symmetry
  • slide
  • reflection.

Area

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • area
  • cover
  • surface
  • measure
  • row/column
  • grid
  • gap
  • overlap
  • unit
  • estimate.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Representing numbers in a variety of ways is essential for developing number sense.

Students can represent numbers using:

Representation typeExample
Number wordsfive
Numerals5
Finger patterns
Collections of perceptual items5 pencils

As a student learns to represent whole numbers, they begin to move between the number words used in counting, numerals and quantity. Students could use concrete materials, gestures (such as nodding) or body tallying (Butterworth 1999) to indicate the count. A student should be able to select a given number of items (more than five) from a larger collection if the number is represented by a word or symbol. For example, a student is shown the numeral 8, and counts out eight items from a collection of twenty items.

The cardinality principle recognises that the last number name represents the total number in the collection. This principle marks a profound conceptual achievement, understanding how counting works (Paliwal and Baroody 2018).

Teaching advice

Counting

Counting is an important component of number knowledge and the early learning of operations. In Early Stage 1, typical development would be for students to be able to count to 30 and elaborate the count by stating the next number without restarting the count.

Counting develops over time as number words are assigned progressively more sophisticated meanings. The process of learning to count, which starts with memorising a few words of the counting list and continues to the point of understanding the cardinality principle, is the process by which students develop their first mental representations of exact, larger numerical quantities (as high as they can count) (Sarnecka et al. 2015).

Counting with understanding

Counting with understanding involves:

  • counting with one-to-one correspondence (one-to-one principle)
  • recognising that the last number name represents the total number in the collection (cardinal principle).

Other counting principles include:

  • stable-order principle: you always say number words in a particular sequence when counting
  • order-irrelevance principle: the order in which you count items does not change the total counted
  • abstraction principle: it does not matter what you count, numbers can be used to count anything and the process for counting is always the same.

There is a distinction between counting by rote and counting with understanding. A student might produce the correct sequence of number words to 15. The same student may not understand the one-to-one correspondence between the number words and the number of objects. It is important to assess one-to-one correspondence and cardinality within a student’s counting range.

When students are learning to count, they can often produce a higher rote count than the largest collection they can count to with understanding. This is why the rote count expectation is at least 30, while students are expected to only represent numbers to at least 20.

Explicit modelling and multiple opportunities for guided and independent practice can support the development of the cardinality principle. Counting a set of objects followed by emphasising the last word counted, and then repeating the final word in the count while gesturing to the corresponding objects can support this understanding (Paliwal and Baroody 2018).

Distinguishing between teens and multiples of ten

The teen numbers in English are often the most difficult for students. The oral language of teen numbers is the reverse of the usual pattern of 'tens first and then ones'.

Students should learn to distinguish between commonly confused similar-sounding numerals, such as 13 and 30 or 15 and 50. Phonemic awareness can assist students in moving between numerals and number words (Lopes-Silva et al. 2014).

Although students in Early Stage 1 are not expected to count sequentially beyond 30, many students may be able to count by tens (10, 20, 30, 40, 50 …). It is important to make the distinction between the suffixes teen and ty as early as possible to reduce the risk of confusing number names when counting higher.

Subitising

The word 'subitise' is derived from Latin and means 'to arrive suddenly'. Subitising is immediately recognising the number of objects in a small (up to four) random collection without having to count the objects. For up to four items, response times increase by about 40–100 ms for every dot, while for larger numbers they increase by 250–350 ms per dot, leading to a clear change in the slope of the response curve (Mandler and Shebo 1982).

It enables us to use grouping structures when establishing the number of items in larger collections.

Perceptual subitising has two different forms:

  • preverbal subitising – does not require naming the number of objects. For example, infants are thought to use preverbal subitising to distinguish between magnitudes, before they learn to speak (Tan and Bryant 2000).
  • verbal subitising – number words express quantity.

Pattern recognition, sometimes referred to as ‘conceptual subitising’ (Clements, 1999), can assist students to develop capabilities of recognising units and combining numbers.

We can also recognise larger numbers of dots when presented in a known pattern (such as the figure below). Many students may initially see this as groups of three.

Figure 1: A collection of dots in a known pattern.

To support the development of subitising, students should develop an understanding that quantities have names. Students should understand that number words have useful purposes for counting and for comparisons (Staves 2019). 

Students who have already demonstrated the cardinality principle and subitising could be extended in their learning by focusing on the pattern structure of numbers through dice and domino patterns and through representing quantities to 20.

Language

The oral count starts as a fixed recitation of number words. It then progresses through overlapping phases of acquiring and elaborating the counting sequence. In the elaboration phase, students learn to continue the count from any point, identifying the number word that comes before or after any counting word.

The challenges of learning the teen number words in English mean that students can often identify which number word comes before twenty-three, in advance of identifying the number word before thirteen.

Languages other than English often have different patterns for number words. Acknowledging the structure of number words in students’ home language will be important in supporting students to understand representations of number in English. Explicit teaching of patterns of number words in English, paired with verbal and visual representations, can assist.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate: 

  • count forwards
  • count backwards
  • number after/number before
  • one less/one more
  • zero
  • number words
  • numerals
  • is the same
  • count
  • pattern
  • ones
  • coins.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to investigate if a student can read and represent whole numbers to at least 20.

  • Provide the student with a shuffled set of number cards (1 to 20).
  • Ask the student to put the numbers in order from smallest to largest. For some students, ordering the cards may include gesture, eye gaze, or verbally telling the teacher.

If the student is unsuccessful, ask the student to count for you. Have the student start from one or two numbers before the initial error in ordering the cards.

If the student is successful, indicate different cards and ask, What number is that?

How the student responds to these questions will provide information on which numerals (1 to 20) they can identify. You could assess numeral recognition by asking the student to indicate various numbers as you say them.

For students with diverse needs this task could be adapted for determining numeral recognition, identification and meaning. This could be done using matching activities, where students are presented with a sample (for example the numeral 5) and a number of pictures to select from (including one correct image). Start with one or two incorrect pictures, increasing as the student becomes proficient. Incorrect pictures could include blank cards, images of larger or smaller quantities and then numbers.

To check if a student demonstrates an understanding of how whole numbers indicate quantity, cover over the first five cards. Ask the student:

How many numbers have I covered up?

[Prompt, if needed] Look at the numbers that are left.

How do you know?

Does the student need to count from one to determine how many are covered? Or does the student recognise that if 6 is visible, 1 to 5 are covered?

Reasoning that five cards have been covered, based on what remains uncovered, suggests an understanding of how whole numbers indicate quantity.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Teachers should encourage students to develop efficient grouping strategies when counting large collections. For example, they can count out groups of five or ten and then find the total using the groups. Grouping makes it easier to check the total.

By combining quantities in a variety of ways, students can learn there are more efficient ways to total large collections than counting one by one.

Teaching advice

A unit of ten things is considered to be a composite unit if it can be interpreted as both one 10 (a single unit) and ten individual units at the same time.

Numeral zero

The numeral 0 plays two separate roles in reading numbers:

  • a lexical tag on the end of a number generating its name, eg 20, 100
  • internal zeros used as place holders, eg 107.

The number line

The number line can be a powerful model for thinking about quantities. To be most effective, the number line needs to be introduced when students can make use of its defining feature – length.

When numeral cards are placed in order side by side they form a numeral track. A numeral track is an ordered sequence of whole numbers. It acts as a counting model because the numerals in the track support counting.

The number line is a more sophisticated model of number. It introduces the idea of distance between numbers. The number line is a model of length. With a number line, students have to count the length units and not the numerals.

Figure 4: An example of a number line (0–9) with a length of 5 shown from zero to 5.

In Geometric measure, students are encouraged to make a measuring device with uniform units before using a ruler. A similar approach can be used to introduce the number line.

Students need both knowledge of numerals and the quantities they represent to use number lines.

Language

In Australia, the word and is used when reading a number greater than 100 or writing it in words.

For example, five hundred and sixty-three.

Students should be made aware that when numbers are used as labels they are said differently. For example:

  • bus numbers
  • postcodes
  • telephone numbers.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • count forwards/count backwards
  • number before/number after
  • more than/less than
  • number line/numeral track
  • digit
  • zero
  • tens/groups of ten
  • round to
  • counters
  • coins
  • dollars/cents
  • odd/even.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

Acquiring an understanding of whole numbers does not develop uniformly. As well as learning the sequence of number names for multiples of 10 to successfully cross the decades, students need experience with the sequence beyond 100.

It is not unusual for students to be uncertain of what number follows 109 (Gould 2017). Teachers may use the following strategies to determine if a student can identify the repeating pattern of counting numbers beyond 100.

  • Ask the student: What number comes after 109?
  • Alternatively, ask the student to: Start counting from 106 and stop at 120.

As students need to learn how to represent numbers using numerals, you could also ask them to record the number that comes after 109. Answers like ‘10010’ for one hundred and ten are attempts at literal transcoding.

content.value:
Why is it important?

Developing and retaining mental images of objects is an important skill for students. Manipulation of a variety of real three-dimensional geometric objects and two-dimensional shapes supports the development of relevant mathematical language and representation. Opportunities for these kinds of activities occur in the classroom, the playground and outside the school. Investigating the type of three-dimensional objects that are stackable makes use of the features of geometric objects in quantifying volume.

Teaching advice

Volume

The attribute of volume is the amount of space occupied by an object. Students in Stage 1 need experience in constructing volumes using informal units such as cubic blocks. Volume is formally measured in later stages using cubic units, such as:

  • cubic centimetres (cm3)
  • cubic metres (m3).

Internal volume (capacity)

Internal volume (capacity) refers to the amount a container can hold and is only used in relation to containers. It generally refers to liquid measurement, that is, the amount of liquid is equal to the internal volume of a container. Students in Stage 1 need experience in filling containers with: 

  • continuous materials such as water
  • discrete objects such as marbles.

Internal volume is formally measured in later stages using units, such as:

  • millilitres (mL)
  • litres (L).

Language

3D objects

The terms used to describe the dimensions of three-dimensional objects take different forms. Although ‘length’, ‘width’ and ‘height’ are commonly used for the three dimensions, the term ‘depth’ is sometimes used in place of height, particularly when referring to an internal dimension.

In everyday use, the context guides our choice of terms:

  • the ‘length’ of a piece of string
  • the ‘width’ of a doorway
  • the ‘height’ of a building
  • the ‘depth’ of a pool.

However, in describing an object that can readily change its orientation such as a wooden block, the choice of labels is not fixed. What would be described as the ‘height’ of the block will depend on how it is positioned.

The terms ‘length’, ‘width’ and ‘height’ can be introduced when students are engaged in using rectangular prisms.

In geometry, the term ‘face’ refers to a flat surface with only straight edges, as in prisms and pyramids. For example, a cube has six faces.

Curved surfaces, such as those found in cones, cylinders and spheres, are not classified as faces. Similarly, flat surfaces with curved boundaries, such as the circular surfaces of cones and cylinders, are not faces.

Internal volume (capacity)

When working with students in Stage 1 it is recommended that the terms ‘capacity’ and ‘internal volume’ be used interchangeably.

The internal volume of a closed container will be slightly less than its volume. Internal volume is based on the inside dimensions, while volume is determined by the outside dimensions of the container.

It is not necessary to refer to these definitions with students as capacity is not taught as a concept separate from volume until Stage 4.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • object
  • cube
  • cylinder
  • sphere
  • flat/curved surface
  • face
  • edge
  • prism
  • internal volume/capacity
  • has more/has less
  • measure.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Describing the data and its spread, as well as creating data displays, draws upon students’ skills in quantitative and spatial reasoning. Comparing probabilities relies on and can support the development of proportional reasoning. When students need to reason beyond the available data, the ideas of chance or likelihood are introduced. Further, comparing probabilities relies on proportional reasoning.

Teaching advice

In Early Stage 1, students collect information about themselves and their environment with teacher assistance. They use objects as data and group these objects into a data display. Objects should be grouped according to characteristics, such as colour, size, shape or texture. Students begin to reason about relations by applying their counting knowledge and skills in comparing the size of different groups of objects.

As students learn to predict responses to and respond to questions about information collected, they begin to develop an introductory understanding of probability. Probability can be a rather challenging concept to grasp as the outcome of many events cannot be predicted with total certainty. Developing a widely acceptable definition of probability took nearly three centuries and was marked by much controversy. In simple terms, probability is how likely something is to happen.

Probability can appear to work against our sense of balance. If a coin has landed heads five times in a row, we expect it to be more likely to turn up tails on the next throw. The idea that what has happened in the past has no impact on the future is challenging for students to understand at this stage of learning. The understanding of chance situations is developed through the use of simple experiments which produce data so that students can make comparisons. However, students’ personal beliefs, such as favourite colours, influence their predictions of chance events. In Early Stage 1, some chance experiments may be included as part of an investigation that collects data.

Students will need support in understanding the key vocabulary demands associated with probability, provided below.

Language

The language of chance is introduced in Early Stage 1 through discussions of data collected. Discussing possible outcomes of data collections can help clarify events that are certain and those that are not.

Question starters include:

  • Could it be …?
  • Why couldn’t it be …?

Using events that are familiar to students will support their understanding of events that are certain and events that are not certain.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • information
  • collect
  • group
  • display
  • objects.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Learning about position is important in locating one’s self and others in space. The words used in describing position are the basis of the prepositions in English, such as ‘in’, ‘on’ or ‘under’. In the early years, learning about length is key to developing an understanding of proximity and provides a useful context for learning about fractions.

Teaching advice

Position

The language and associated vocabulary developed regarding position are important both within the topic of position itself, and for use with other mathematical concepts. Words and phrases such as ‘next to’, ‘before’ and ‘after’ can be used both in a physical world context and also in more abstract contexts. For example, in position – the chair is next to the table or the teacher entered the room before the students, whereas in number – 13 comes before 14, or 20 is next to 19 on the chart.

Positional language should be addressed regularly to enable students to develop a deep understanding of when and how to use these words. A variety of physical, digital and visual representations are helpful for some phrases such as ‘on top of’. On top of can be difficult as students may be confused between whether it means superimposed or above (see images below).

There are two main ideas associated with position for students in Early Stage 1:

  • following an instruction to position an object or themselves
  • describing the relative position of an object or themselves.

Some students may be able to describe the position of an object in relation to themselves, but not in relation to another object. The concept of position has strong vocabulary demands that are detailed below.

Ordinals

Ordinal number words such as ‘first’, ‘second’ and ‘third' represent a position in a sequence. They are different from whole numbers, which represent quantity. Ordinal numbers are introduced in relevant contexts, such as games, storytelling or recording the date.

Left and right

In Early Stage 1, students learn to use the terms ‘left’ and ‘right’ to describe position in relation to themselves. Teachers can assist students’ understanding of left and right by referencing a dominant hand or foot. The terms ‘left’ and ‘right’ depend on the frame of reference (which way an individual is facing) and can be a source of confusion for several years.

Typically, students are not expected to use ‘left’ or ‘right’ to describe the position of an object from the perspective of a person facing in the opposite direction until Stage 1. However, students who have mastered the concept of left and right in relation to themselves might be introduced to this idea.

Some students with perceptual difficulties and poor spatial awareness may experience difficulties with the concept of position. Modelling, and the use of visual cues, can support these students to follow or describe position.

Conversely, some students have well-developed skills in applying the concept of position, even if they do not yet have the language to articulate it. For example, some Aboriginal students may demonstrate a high degree of spatial awareness on a larger scale, such as in the local area or on-Country. Students may be supported by explicit teaching of mathematical language associated with spatial positioning.

Length

Early Stage 1 students often develop an awareness of the attribute of length by comparing objects of different lengths. Early Stage 1 focuses on the importance of accurately aligning one end of each object being compared. Where possible, students need experience with physically aligning the ends of two objects to compare their lengths. Start with comparing objects where the difference in lengths is easy to notice, for example the table is longer than the pencil. 

When items are closer in length, aligning the ends becomes necessary. For example comparing the height of two students by standing them back-to-back or aligning the ends of the two pencils.

Conservation of length is an important concept. It develops over time when students are comparing lengths. If students consistently say that the objects are equal in length, though their relative positions have been altered, they are conserving length.

Introducing fractions through length

Many students find understanding fractions, and particularly fraction magnitudes, to be one of the most challenging concepts in mathematics. The concept of a fraction is based on the process of division, rather than counting parts. To assist students in developing the process of division and its relationship to fractions, the continuous linear model of fractions is addressed in the concept of length.

The syllabus introduces fractions through equal sharing, using continuous and discrete models. This lays the foundations for fractions as indicating division and fractions as numbers.

Half

Half can be interpreted as dividing one whole into two equal pieces (continuous) or dividing a collection into two equal groups (discrete). The process is applied in early models of halving lengths and discrete quantities.

See Forming groups for discrete models of fractions.

The idea of a halfway point builds on the equality of two lengths. It also introduces the notion of subdividing a length, which in turn underpins measuring. It is important to model and reinforce the language of two equal lengths when describing ‘halfway’ and to provide non-examples where the lengths are not equal.

Further advice is available in Introducing fractions: Sharing (linked with division).

Some students with poor visual perception and difficulties with fine motor skills may require additional support to manipulate items and compare lengths. Strategies that can support these students include:

  • using visual cues such as a sticker or object to indicate the start and end of lengths
  • outlining boundaries of an image in bold
  • selecting colours that give a good colour contrast between background and foreground if using images of lengths
  • participating in activities that require hand–eye coordination.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of length and half a length, could be extended in their learning by finding other fractions of lengths such as repeatedly halving to find quarters, or exploring folding to make thirds.

Language

Students may need practice with the language of length in a variety of contexts. Young students often use general terms such as ‘big’ when they mean ‘tall’. They may know the word ‘fat’, but not the word ‘thick’. The terms ‘big’ and ‘long’ are sometimes used for specific attributes such as:

  • height
  • width
  • depth
  • length
  • thickness.

Engage students in activities that develop clarity in expressing distinct mathematical concepts. Providing examples and non-examples, including through the use of the Frayer model, can support students’ understanding of these mathematical concepts. See Vocabulary and language in Mathematics K–6 (Word, 16 pages, 1.14MB) for a further explanation, examples and non-examples.

Teachers can support students to use the language of mathematics by developing understanding that the same word can be used in a range of contexts. Some students may use ‘big’ to signify importance or ‘biggest’ to indicate intensity, such as those who use Aboriginal English. Making connections between concepts, and ensuring that students know when the context is mathematical, can support students to select the most appropriate term to use.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • position
  • between/next to/behind
  • inside/outside
  • left/right
  • directions
  • length
  • end/end to end
  • side by side
  • long/longer than/longest
  • short/shorter than/shortest
  • high/higher than/highest
  • tall/taller than/tallest
  • low/lower than/lowest
  • the same as
  • near/nearer
  • far/further
  • close/closer
  • whole
  • equal parts
  • half/halves/about halfway
  • more than a half/less than a half.

system.name: MS ES1 Teaching advice for Geometric measure

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

The units of measurement in Mass (g, kg) and Time (min, sec) do not rely on a physical spatial structure. In Mass, the spatial arrangement of the units does not affect the total weight. This is different to area or length where the arrangement of the units matter – they need to be end to end with no gaps.

In Early Stage 1, it is important that students develop an awareness of the attribute of mass and some of the language used to describe mass.

Concepts of time and duration are influenced by students’ experiences, cultural knowledge and personal judgements. Time can be understood and represented in a range of ways such as lunar, seasonal and Gregorian calendar systems, or linear and cyclical concepts of time.

Teaching advice

While Mass and Time are organised under the same substrand, it is not intended that teachers make connections across concepts in each of Time and Mass.

Mass

Early experiences often lead students to the conclusion that:

  • large things are heavier than small things, and
  • if two things are the same size and shape, they will have the same mass.

However, mass is not a spatial measure. Objects with the same volume can have different masses.

Students in Early Stage 1 should only be asked to compare two objects that are quite different in mass. Students need experiences with objects that are:

  • light and large
  • heavy and large
  • light and small
  • heavy and small
  • large but lighter than a smaller object.

Recognising that students may have different gross motor skills, teachers may need to provide a variety of experiences in order to support students to experience mass. These experiences could include:

  • feeling resistance against the body to determine if something is heavy or light
  • using grip to identify the mass of an object, using the terms ‘lighter’ or ‘heavier’
  • placing an object, such as a blanket, on the student’s lap to determine if the object is light or heavy.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of mass could be extended in their learning by exploring the placement of mass at different points on an equal-arm balance.

Time

Duration

An understanding of duration is introduced through ideas such as:

  • before
  • after
  • how long
  • how soon.

In Early Stage 1 time spans are personal judgements. Moments in time include ideas such as:

  • daytime
  • today
  • days of the week.

Students can be supported to develop an understanding of time by introducing time in everyday contexts, for example:

  • wait times for activities
  • duration of preferred activities, eg using timers
  • schedule of familiar routines, eg first-and-then board, visual schedule
  • identifying days of the week through regular weekly routines, eg sports, music
  • identifying activities done before and after school, eg night-time routines.

Telling time

In Early Stage 1, telling time focuses on reading hour time on analog and digital clocks. It draws on:

  • numeral recognition
  • position
  • spatial comparison.

Analog and digital clocks can be shown either through real objects or visual representations. When engaging with analog or digital clocks, it is important to ensure these displays are accessible. Consider using:

  • strong colour contrast between the hour and minute hands to improve visibility
  • braille, tactile or talking clocks.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of time could be extended in their learning by representing times on analog and digital clocks.

Schools are encouraged to work in partnership with their local Aboriginal community(ies) to develop understanding about Aboriginal concepts of time and associated language and terminology. This can assist teachers to support students in developing their understanding of content related to time.

Language

The terms ‘weigh’ and ‘weight’ are more common in everyday usage than ‘mass’. When working with students in Early Stage 1 ‘weight’ is an acceptable description for mass. Weight is a force that changes with gravity, while mass remains constant.

Hefting is testing the weight of an object by lifting or holding and balancing it. Where possible, students can use their bodies to balance two objects and compare the weight of each, for example holding one object in each hand.

The words ‘long’ and ‘short’ can be confusing to students who have only experienced these words in terms of length measurement. Students need experience with these words in both the context of length and time. Teachers should be mindful that the terms ‘long’ and ‘short’ are comparatives. Students might consider 5 years, 5 000 years, or 50 000 years to be a long time.

Some students, including Aboriginal students, may distinguish historical from contemporary time scales. For example, students may use additional qualifiers or alternative terms, such as ‘very long’, ‘long, long time ago’ or ‘old time’.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • mass
  • matter
  • heavy/heavier/heaviest
  • light/lighter/lightest
  • about the same as
  • hard to push/hard to pull
  • daytime/night-time
  • yesterday/today/tomorrow
  • before/after/next
  • a long time/a short time
  • days/week
  • weekdays/weekend days
  • time
  • morning/afternoon
  • clock
  • analog/digital
  • hands (of a clock)
  • o'clock.

system.name: MS ES1 Teaching advice for Non-spatial measure

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Concepts related to three-dimensional space are important to functioning in the world. Three-dimensional spatial structure is foundational for developing skills and processes related to position and location, perspective, and directions.

The manipulation of a variety of 3D objects supports the development of visual imagery, language and representation. Manipulation of 3D objects and observing them from different viewpoints leads to the development of skills in identifying the structural features of objects.

Students learn to understand volume as related to the measurement of three-dimensional space, in the same way that area relates to the measurement of two-dimensional space. Students need to explore the concept of volume as part of identifying and quantifying attributes of an object. Learning to compare internal volumes of containers and volumes of objects (how much space they take up) develops important estimation skills.

Teaching advice

3D geometric objects

In Early Stage 1, the emphasis is on students manipulating, describing, sorting and representing familiar geometric objects. Teachers are encouraged to use a range of objects of different sizes. Some students may require larger objects to manipulate.

Students should also be encouraged to describe the features of familiar objects using the terms ‘flat’, ‘round’ or ‘curved’. This prepares students to sort objects based on particular attributes, such as size, shape or function.

In developing students’ skills in reasoning about spatial relations, students should engage in tasks where they predict the stacking capabilities of various objects.

Volume and internal volume (capacity)

The attribute of volume is the amount of space occupied by an object or substance. The internal volume or capacity is only used in relation to containers and generally refers to liquid measurement. Knowing these definitions is not an expectation at this stage in learning.

In Early Stage 1, comparisons are made directly, using methods such as pouring or packing the contents of one container into another. Students can engage in pouring and filling containers with water or sand.

Early experiences often lead students to the conclusion that taller containers hold more. To develop beyond this, students need to directly compare containers that are:

  • shorter and hold more
  • taller and hold less
  • shorter and hold less
  • taller and hold more
  • short and hold the same as a tall container.

Many opportunities to emphasise the concepts of volume and capacity occur throughout the school day.

Students may be involved in stacking objects:

  • packing up toys
  • making models
  • storing objects in cupboards.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of volume could be extended in their learning by exploring different ways of stacking 24 cubes (eg 3 by 2 by 4 or 6 by 2 by 2).

Language

Students often need meaningful practice in using the general word container to include objects such as bottles, jars and tubs.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • object
  • shape
  • size
  • curved/flat
  • pointy/round
  • roll/slide
  • stack
  • container
  • liquid
  • empty/full/about half full
  • volume
  • space
  • has more/has less
  • will hold more/will hold less
  • takes up more space.

system.name: MS ES1 Teaching advice for Three-dimensional spatial structure

images.description: Line drawing of a chevron shape.
Line drawing of a kite shape.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

The development of two-dimensional spatial structure includes an ability to identify, rotate, orient and visualise shapes. These spatial skills are foundational for developing mathematical understanding related to the array structure of multiplication and area, map interpretation, visualisation and geometric reasoning (Lowrie et al. 2021). 

Features and properties of shapes also contribute to understanding the connection between two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects and spaces.

Students entering Early Stage 1 typically bring an understanding of shapes, which includes both regular and irregular shapes. In Early Stage 1, students also develop an awareness of the attribute of area through covering activities. Students’ knowledge and skills in spatial reasoning develop as they engage with content related to shape and area.

Teaching advice

2D shape

Students should be given time to explore and represent shapes in a range of contexts, such as:

  • identifying shapes in the classroom, school and local environment
  • representing shapes through painting, drawing, movements, gestures, writing, cutting and pasting.

It is important to select or create images of shapes that give a good colour contrast between background and foreground. This will assist students to see the images clearly and support students with visual difficulties.

Features of shapes

Children first learn that the question, What shape is this? is answered by words such as ‘circle’ and ‘square’. They then associate these shape words with initial examples. The initial examples contribute to the prototype image students hold for a shape. The equilateral triangle is a common prototype image for a triangle. This has meant that some students identify a right-angled triangle as half a triangle (Hourigan and Leavy 2015). For this reason it is important for teachers to introduce all types of triangles.

To develop a robust concept of shapes it is important that students encounter shapes in different orientations and sizes, represented in a variety of ways. Templates from which students create shapes can help to reinforce their understanding of the features of shapes and support developing students’ skills in reasoning about spatial relations.

Non-examples

In addition to showing students examples of a shape, providing non-examples of the shape helps focus their attention on the critical attributes. The non-examples should be similar to the examples, but without the defining characteristic of the shapes.

For example, a triangle with the defining characteristic of the number of sides, could be compared to:

Shape NameShape
Chevron
Kite

Students who require additional support to identify shapes may first need to be introduced to non-examples with significantly different characteristics. Match-to-sample activities can also support the understanding of the features of particular shapes. Students can be presented with a correct sample and one or two non-examples to begin with, with the number of non-examples increasing as students’ understanding develops.

In Early Stage 1, students should work with asymmetric or irregular shapes as well as regular shapes. Students are not expected to use the terms ‘regular’ and ‘irregular’ themselves.

See Vocabulary and language in Mathematics K–6 (Word, 16 pages, 1.14MB) for a further explanation of teaching concepts using examples and non-examples.

Area

Students should be given opportunities to compare:

  • two similar shapes of different areas where one fits inside the boundary of the other
  • two different-shaped areas where one can be placed on top of the other
  • two different shapes with the same area where one shape can be cut up and pasted onto the other.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of area could be extended in their learning by:

  • comparing shapes with similar areas that cannot be superimposed on each other
  • predicting and finding two shapes that might have the same area
  • learning to measure area.

Language

The term ‘shape’ is used in the syllabus to refer to a two-dimensional figure. ‘Object’ is used to refer to a three-dimensional solid or geometric form.

There are two different strategies that students can use to compare area by placing one on top of another. These are: superimposing and superposing.

Superimpose: comparison of areas by placing one area on top of another. 

Superpose: comparison of areas by aligning the edges (or corners) of two areas when one is placed on top of the other. 

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • shape/closed shape
  • circle
  • triangle
  • square
  • rectangle
  • features
  • side
  • line/curve
  • area
  • surface
  • inside/outside
  • bigger than/smaller than/the same as.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

A chance event is something that happens without a clear cause. Randomness is a difficult concept to grasp, even for adults. We tend to see patterns in data, even where none exist. By the end of Stage 1 students should typically be able to acknowledge the existence of a range of possible outcomes for an event. They should also be able to express the idea that some events are more likely to occur than others.

Teaching advice

Encourage students to recognise the impact of chance on predictions they make.

Certainty

When considering certainty, there are two extremes:

  • events that are certain to happen
  • events that are certain not to happen.

Words such as 'might', 'may' and 'possible' describe events between these two extremes.

Students often need assistance to develop an understanding of the terms ‘certain’ or ‘impossible’. Some students interpret events with a low probability as being impossible.

The idea of impossible, particularly in social contexts, is a more difficult concept for students than more likely or equally likely. Although we might not expect a coin toss to result in a coin standing on its edge, it is not impossible. It is the aggregation of all of the possible outcomes that really means an event is certain or impossible.

Sample space

To address notions of chance, it is often best to use examples where all the things that can happen, sometimes called the sample space, are well defined. Students often do not realise that for something to be impossible there must be none present at all in the sample space, the set of all possible outcomes. Determining the sample space (that is, what is possible) is the essential first step in understanding any probability problem.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • possible
  • might happen
  • likely/unlikely/more likely.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

In society, there is a constant need to understand, interpret and analyse information displayed in tables or graphical forms. Students need to recognise how information may be displayed in a misleading way, resulting in drawing the wrong conclusions about the data. Experiences with collecting, organising, displaying, and analysing data assist students in developing graphical and statistical literacy skills (Watson and Callingham 2003).

Early experiences with data should be based on real-life contexts relevant to the students and connected to other curriculum areas such as History, Geography, or Science and Technology. Students should be encouraged to ask questions relevant to their experiences and interests and to design ways of investigating their questions. Students develop effective data collection and display methods to present data in a variety of ways.

Teaching advice

Representing an object with a different object, picture or drawing is an abstraction.

It is important that each object in a (one-to-one) data display represents one object. One object can also represent an idea, such as a person's preference.

Aligning the rows or columns of images to form a common baseline in a picture graph can make comparisons easier.

Collecting data

When collecting information to investigate a question, students can develop simple ways of recording. Some methods include:

  • placing blocks or counters in a line
  • colouring squares on grid paper
  • using tally marks.

Tally marks

A single mark in a tally represents 1 observation. Tally marks are usually drawn in groups of five. The first four marks are often drawn vertical, with the fifth mark drawn diagonally through the first four. This makes counting in groups more efficient. For example:

Tally marksRepresents
3
5
9

Different countries use different systems of tally marks. Cultures using Chinese characters tally five by making 正.

Data in categories

Categorical data means the information being collected can be separated into distinct groups or categories. Examples include:

  • the colours of Smarties in a box
  • class members’ favourite fruits.

Students may engage more effectively with collecting data through observation or conversation, rather than questioning. Some Aboriginal students, for a number of cultural and historical reasons, may prefer not to ask or be asked direct questions, or may have well-developed observational skills that could be applied through learning activities related to collecting data.

Some students may experience difficulty accessing visual representations of data. These students can be supported by presenting data in alternate formats and through the use of assistive technology, including screen readers.

When using visual texts such as images, picture graphs, lists and tables, it is important to ensure these are accessible. Consider using:

  • strong colour contrast to improve visibility
  • alternative text and captions to provide descriptions.

Some students may also experience difficulty with conceptually understanding visual representations of data. In these instances, visual information can be introduced to students using their preferred method of communication, for example:

  • real objects
  • photos of real objects
  • images of objects
  • abstract images or drawings.

This provides opportunities for students to develop their understanding of the language used in data displays and attribute meaning between the visual representation and the data.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • information
  • data
  • collect
  • gather
  • display
  • symbol
  • tally mark
  • picture graph.

Representing an object with a different object, picture or drawing is an abstraction.

It is important that each object in a (one-to-one) data display represents one object. One object can also represent an idea, such as a person's preference.

Aligning the rows or columns of images to form a common baseline in a picture graph can make comparisons easier.

Collecting data

When collecting information to investigate a question, students can develop simple ways of recording. Some methods include:

  • placing blocks or counters in a line
  • colouring squares on grid paper
  • using tally marks.

Tally marks

A single mark in a tally represents 1 observation. Tally marks are usually drawn in groups of five. The first four marks are often drawn vertical, with the fifth mark drawn diagonally through the first four. This makes counting in groups more efficient. For example:

Tally marksRepresents
3
5
9

Different countries use different systems of tally marks. Cultures using Chinese characters tally five by making 正.

Data in categories

Categorical data means the information being collected can be separated into distinct groups or categories. Examples include:

  • the colours of Smarties in a box
  • class members’ favourite fruits.

Students may engage more effectively with collecting data through observation or conversation, rather than questioning. Some Aboriginal students, for a number of cultural and historical reasons, may prefer not to ask or be asked direct questions, or may have well-developed observational skills that could be applied through learning activities related to collecting data.

Some students may experience difficulty accessing visual representations of data. These students can be supported by presenting data in alternate formats and through the use of assistive technology, including screen readers.

When using visual texts such as images, picture graphs, lists and tables, it is important to ensure these are accessible. Consider using:

  • strong colour contrast to improve visibility
  • alternative text and captions to provide descriptions.

Some students may also experience difficulty with conceptually understanding visual representations of data. In these instances, visual information can be introduced to students using their preferred method of communication, for example:

  • real objects
  • photos of real objects
  • images of objects
  • abstract images or drawings.

This provides opportunities for students to develop their understanding of the language used in data displays and attribute meaning between the visual representation and the data.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • information
  • data
  • collect
  • gather
  • display
  • symbol
  • tally mark
  • picture graph.

Why is it important?

Forming groups helps students progress from counting by ones to skip counting and using repeated addition. These are important steps towards the idea of coordinating units and understanding multiplication.

Teaching advice

Rhythmic and skip counting

Number words sequences for fives and tens produce a rhythm. This rhythm can be used in choral counting. Skip counting by two can develop from counting aloud and:

  • stressing each second number: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 …
  • skipping over the non-stressed numbers: 2, 4, 6 …

Division

There are two forms of division associated with forming groups:

DivisionTypeMeaningExample
Equal SharingPartitiveHow many in each group?If 12 marbles are shared between three students, how many does each student get?
Equal groupingQuotitiveHow many groups are there?If I have 12 marbles and each child is to get four, how many children will get marbles?

Understanding grouping division is important to make sense of dividing by a quantity less than one (eg 8 ÷ 0·5) which students encounter in Stage 4.

After students have divided a quantity into equal groups (eg twelve objects divided into groups of four) they should recombine the groups. This reversal of the process links multiplication and division.

When sharing a collection of objects into two groups, students may describe the number of objects in each group as being one half of the whole collection.

Arrays

An array is one of several different arrangements that can be used to model multiplicative situations involving whole numbers.

An array is made by arranging a set of objects, such as counters or pictures, into columns and rows:

  • each column must contain the same number of items as the other columns
  • each row must contain the same number of items as the other rows.

Students should focus on using groups of, before progressing to rows of and columns of. Although the array is a powerful mathematical model, it requires students to identify groups in two directions. Coordinating between columns and rows is much more difficult than using groups of with repeated addition.

Composite units

A composite unit is a unit-whole composed of other units. A unit of 10 things is a composite unit if it can be interpreted as both one 10 (a single unit) and 10 individual units at the same time. A model of a composite unit would be one pea pod containing 10 peas.

In developing an understanding of a group acting as composite it is helpful to distinguish between the number of groups and the number in each group as this can be confusing for students.

Introducing fractions: Equal sharing (linked with division)

Many students find understanding fractions, and in particular fraction magnitudes, one of the most challenging concepts in learning mathematics.

Fractions are introduced through equal-sharing problems. As Empson and Levi (2011) stated, ‘If models do not draw on children’s formative experiences of sharing and partitioning, then they are likely to prevent teachers from cultivating the natural insights about quantities that young children have’.

Students can later connect the words and symbols for fractions to the parts created in the process of solving the problems. The concept of a fraction is then based on the process of division, rather than counting parts. This lays the foundations for fractions as indicating division and fractions as numbers.

Equal sharing begins with sharing between two. The process of halving is applied in early models of halving lengths (see Geometric measure) and discrete quantities in forming groups. To assist students in seeing the link between the two models, linear arrangements of discrete quantities are used.

Some students may have prior knowledge and understanding of fractions and dividing objects equally among groups. For example, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students may have an understanding of the concept of fractions as it relates to kinship and community responsibilities.

Language

Check that students are familiar with groups of two like things being called pairs.

Avoid using the term ‘lots of’ when describing grouping for multiplication. It can be confusing to students because of its everyday use, for example ‘lots of fish in the sea'.

Formal writing of number sentences for multiplication and division, including the use of the symbols × and ÷ is not introduced until Stage 2.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to determine if a student can use the structure of equal groups to solve multiplication problems and group for division (this activity was also described in Early Stage 1 Forming groups).

[Provide students with a pile of at least 20 unifix cubes]

Can you make 5 towers, with 3 blocks in each tower?

How many towers do you have?

How many blocks in each tower?

How many altogether?

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • group
  • number of groups/number in each group
  • row/column
  • number of rows/number of columns
  • number in each row/number in each column
  • array
  • sharing/shared between
  • left over
  • total
  • equal
  • half/quarter/eighth
  • one-half/one-quarter/one-eighth
  • halve.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Being able to describe the relative positions of objects in a picture or diagram requires interpretation of a two-dimensional representation. In Stage 1, measuring the lengths of objects using uniform informal units enables students to develop some key understandings of measurement.

Teaching advice

Position

In Early Stage 1, students used the terms ‘left’ and ‘right’ to describe position in relation to themselves. In Stage 1, many students begin to use the terms ‘left’ and ‘right’ to describe position from the perspective of a person facing in the opposite direction.

Length

Understandings involved in measuring the lengths of objects include:

  • units should be repeatedly placed end to end without gaps or overlaps
  • units must be equal in size
  • identical units should be used to compare lengths
  • some units are more appropriate for measuring particular objects
  • there is a relationship between the size of the chosen unit and the number of units needed.

Make, mark and move

Using the phrase make, mark and move assists students in understanding the concept of repeated units. By placing a unit on a flat surface, marking where it ends, moving it along and continuing the process, students identify that the unit of measurement is the space between the marks on a measuring device and not the marks themselves.

Conserving length

Recognising that a length may be divided and recombined to form the same length is an important component of conserving length.

Estimating length

Estimating length is often based on visualising a known unit or benchmark. The units might be personal measures such as finger-widths or handspans.

Before students are asked to estimate lengths and distances it is important that students:

  • have had some measurement experiences
  • are taught a variety of estimation strategies.

To estimate longer distances, teachers may ask students to imagine how many times a metre ruler could be laid end to end across the space. To assist with this method of estimating, have one student measure out the distance being estimated with a metre ruler. Allow students to adjust their estimates after the first metre is measured and again at about halfway.

Students may have prior knowledge or experience with measurement and estimating length. For example, some Aboriginal students may have a sense of measurement based on their cultural knowledge or on-Country experiences. Teachers are encouraged to further develop their knowledge, and engage in meaningful exchange with students to support making connections with Western concepts of measurement.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • length
  • distance
  • end/end to end
  • side by side
  • gap
  • overlap
  • measure
  • estimate
  • unit
  • handspan.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to determine if a student can identify the halfway point of a journey. This question relates to both length and fractions and builds on the content in Early Stage 1.

An ant crawls around the outside of this triangle [teacher gestures around the sides of the triangle]:

If each side of the triangle is the same length, can you show where the ant will be when it is half of the way around the triangle from the start?

Starting from the base emphasises the need to find half of the distance around the triangle rather than halving the triangle.

title.name: 📜 Title
title.value: Teaching advice for Geometric measure A

system.name: MS S1 Teaching advice for Geometric measure A

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Length

Formal units of length

Students should be given opportunities to apply their understanding of measurement, gained through experiences with the use of uniform informal units, to experiences with the use of the centimetre and metre.

They could make a measuring device using uniform informal units before using a ruler, eg using a length of 10 connecting cubes. This would assist students in understanding that the distances between marks on a ruler represent unit lengths and that the marks indicate the endpoints of each unit. Half of a length of 10 connecting cubes provides a link to simple fractions.

Fractional lengths

In Stage 1, fractions are formed by the process of division rather than counting parts. Fractional parts, halves, quarters and eighths are formed in two different ways:

  • equal parts of a whole length
  • equal quantities of a linear arrangement of a collection of objects.

In focusing on repeated halving, emphasise that the size of the resulting fractional part will depend on the size of the original whole length or collection of objects. It is not necessary for students in Stage 1 to use the symbol ½ to mean one-half or use ¼ for one-quarter.

Three models of fractions

Continuous model (linear)

The continuous model (linear) should be introduced first. It uses one-directional cuts or folds that compare fractional parts based on length. It is helpful to highlight the long edge to focus on length.

Continuous model (area)

This model uses multi-directional cuts or folds to compare fractional parts to the whole. This model should be introduced once students understand the concept of area developed in Stage 2. Folding to show equivalent area relies on a shape having an axis of symmetry for the fold line.

Discrete model

This model uses separate items in collections to represent parts of the whole group.

Language

When recording measurements, a space should be left between the number and the abbreviated unit, eg 3 cm, not 3cm.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • metre
  • centimetre.
