system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Properties of geometrical figures C (Path)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Key ideas

Students:

  • identify and define the trigonometric ratios for right-angled triangles and use trigonometric notation
  • find approximations of trigonometric ratios for given angles
  • find the size of an angle given a trigonometric ratio using digital tools
  • select and use appropriate trigonometric ratios to find unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles
  • select and use appropriate trigonometric ratios to find unknown angles in right-angled triangles in degrees and minutes
  • solve problems in a variety of contexts using trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles

Key terms

  • adjacent
  • cosine ratio
  • hypotenuse
  • ratio
  • right angle
  • sine ratio
  • tangent ratio

Background knowledge

  • Rounding numbers to a specified degree of accuracy
  • Describing properties of similar triangles
  • Using degrees as a unit of measurement
  • Classifying triangles according to angle size
  • Using a scientific calculator or equivalent

Making connections

ConnectionsOutcome or Stage
Trigonometric ratios are strongly connected with ratio and scale drawing.Stage 4 Ratios and Rates
Trigonometric ratios are also strongly connected to similar triangles.Stage 5 Properties of Geometrical Figures B
Finding angles using inverse trigonometric ratios links to inverse functions and inverse trigonometric functions.Stage 6 Mathematics Extension
Finding angles in triangles connects to using radian measure.Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced
The tangent ratio can be interpreted as the gradient of a line in the Cartesian plane and can be used to find the angle between a line and the positive 𝑥-axis.

Stage 5 Linear Relationships A

Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced

Trigonometric ratios are used in navigation and bearings.Stage 5 Geography
Trigonometry is used in constructing ramps, buildings and other surfaces that are constructed on sloped ground. Trigonometry was also used in constructing the pyramids, exhibiting almost identical proportions as well as isosceles triangular faces slanted at very similar angles.Real-world applications

Non-routine problem solving

system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Trigonometry A

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Key ideas

Students:

  • identify angles of elevation and depression and solve related problems using trigonometry
  • identify, describe and compare true bearings and compass bearings
  • convert between the 2 representations of bearings
  • solve problems involving bearings in various contexts using trigonometry

Key terms

  • angle of depression
  • angle of elevation
  • compass bearing
  • cosine ratio
  • sine ratio
  • tangent ratio
  • true bearing

Background knowledge

  • Rounding numbers to a specified degree of accuracy
  • Rounding hours, minutes and seconds to a specified degree of accuracy
  • Using Pythagoras’ theorem to find unknown sides
  • Using trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, tangent) in right-angled triangles
  • Using a scientific calculator to calculate with trigonometric ratios
  • Compass directions
  • Properties of angles formed by a transversal on parallel lines and basic angle properties
  • Naming conventions for angles

Making connections

ConnectionsOutcome or Stage
Angles of elevation and depression and bearings all connect to trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles.Stage 5 Trigonometry A
Angles of depression connects to the geometrical property of alternate angles on parallel lines being equal.Stage 4 Angle Relationships
Bearings connects to geometrical properties for angles at a point, complementary and supplementary angles.Stage 4 Angle Relationships
Bearings can be used in three-dimensional trigonometry problems.Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced
Bearings relate to map work, including fieldwork and reading compass bearings or true bearings on maps or measuring instruments.Stage 4, 5 and 6 Geography
The 16 points on a compass (eg SSW) can be connected to compass bearings in everyday life and determining direction on a map.Stage 5 and Stage 6 Geography
Rounding angles to the nearest degree, minute or second can be related to hours, minutes and seconds in time.Stage 3 Time

Non-routine problem solving

  • Design a zip-line to be built in your area. The zip-line can start at a height you pick and should end at ground-level. A safe zip-line should have no more than a 4-degree angle of elevation. Draw a diagram of your zip-line, showing the height of the starting point, the length of the line and the distance covered.
  • Use a clinometer to determine the heights of school buildings or trees and use these results to estimate distances and lengths.
  • Plan a journey or treasure hunt around the school by using a map and bearings.

Further advice is given in support materials which provide teaching strategies, supports and scaffolds demonstrating how to support the diversity of learners in Mathematics 7–10.

Key ideas

  • Pythagoras’ theorem
  • Sine, cosine and tangent ratios in right-angled triangles
  • Substitution into formulas
  • Solving multi-step equations and equations involving fractions

Making connections

ConnectionsOutcome or Stage
The sine rule can be proven using similar triangles, circle geometry or vectors.

Stage 5 Properties of geometrical figures B

Stage 5 Circle Geometry

Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 1

The cosine rule is a generalisation of Pythagoras’ theorem.Stage 4 Pythagoras’ Theorem
The sine and cosine rules are connected to circle geometry theorems concerning angles at the centre and circumference and cyclic quadrilaterals.Stage 5 Circle Geometry
Trigonometry is connected to navigation to determine the distance between a boat and the shore.Stage 5 Trigonometry A
Using the sine rule to find angles from a description may involve the ambiguous case.

Stage 5 Trigonometry D

Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced

Trigonometric identities are used to solve equations and prove and simplify results.

Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced

Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 1

Trigonometry is used in construction to find angles and lengths.Real-world applications
Pythagoras’ theorem and trigonometry are used extensively when working with vectors.Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 1
Pythagoras’ theorem and trigonometry are used extensively to calculate forces and problems involving motion, including projectiles.

Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 1

Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 2

Trigonometry is used when finding the area and perimeter of irregular-shaped paddocks for fencing.Stage 6 Mathematics Standard 2

Non-routine problem solving

  • Derive the formula for the volume of a tetrahedron.
  • A sailor leaves Port A and travels SW at a speed of 20 km/h. After 30 minutes, he does a sharp turn and travels in the direction of 070°T at the same speed. After 45 minutes, how far is the sailor from his starting point?
  • Tom stands at Point A, due south from the base of a tower. He observes the angle of elevation to the top of a tower is 38°. He walks in a straight line, 50 metres to Point B, where he is now standing on a bearing of 070° from the base of the tower. From this point, he observes the top of the tower is at an angle of elevation of 32°. Find the height of the tower correct to the nearest centimetre.
  • Find the angle that one of the triangular faces of a square-based pyramid makes with the horizontal base if the height of the pyramid is 80 m and the base has side length 150 m.
  • Two observers are standing at different locations X and Y on ground level. They are standing 2000 m apart and can see a balloon B in the air, hovering directly above the Point G. The observer standing at X sees the balloon on a bearing of 023°T at an angle of elevation of 24°. The observer standing at Y sees the balloon on a bearing of 335°T at an angle of elevation to be 18°.

Further advice is given in support materials which provide teaching strategies, supports and scaffolds demonstrating how to support the diversity of learners in Mathematics 7–10.

system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Trigonometry C (Path)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Key ideas

Students:

  • prove that the tangent ratio can be expressed as a ratio of the sine and cosine ratios
  • compare the features of sine, cosine and tangent curves from their graphs for angles of any magnitude, including negative angles
  • apply the relationships for obtuse angles
  • apply the sine rule and area rule to find angles involving the ambiguous case
  • relate the gradient of a line to its angle of inclination on the Cartesian plane
  • apply the exact sine, cosine and tangent ratios for angles of 30°, 45° and 60°
  • apply the relationships between the sine and cosine ratios of complementary angles in right-angled triangles
  • find the possible acute and/or obtuse angle(s) given a trigonometric ratio

Key terms

  • acute angle
  • angle of inclination
  • Cartesian plane
  • complementary angles
  • cosine rule
  • obtuse
  • Pythagoras’ theorem
  • sine rule
  • tangent ratio
  • trigonometric ratio
  • unit circle

Background knowledge

Making connections

ConnectionsOutcome or Stage
The unit circle is a circle with centre (0, 0) and radius 1.Stage 5 Non-linear relationships C
The trigonometric functions in terms of the unit circle are used to prove trigonometric identities and are connected to Cartesian and polar coordinates.

Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 1

Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 2

The formula gradient m = tanθ is connected to graphs of straight lines.

Stage 4 Linear relationships

Stage 5 Linear relationships

Trigonometric functions are linked to graphing non-linear relationships and knowledge of functions.

Stage 5 Paths Functions and other graphs

Stage 5 Paths Non-linear Relationships C

Trigonometric functions are connected to circle geometry and Pythagoras’ theorem.

Stage 4 Pythagoras’ Theorem

Stage 5 Circle Geometry

The graphs of the trigonometric functions mark the transition from understanding trigonometry as the study of lengths and angles in triangles to the study of waves.Stage 6 Physics
Trigonometric functions are used to calculate forces, weights, velocity, acceleration, gravitational and magnetic fields. Waves are fundamental to a vast range of physical and practical phenomena like light and other electromagnetic waves and to periodic phenomena like daily temperatures and fluctuating sales over the year.Stage 6 Physics
Reciprocal trigonometric ratios and transformations of trigonometric functions are examined in Stage 6.Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced

Non-routine problem solving

  • Examine the relationship between the sine rule and the diameter of the circumcircle of a triangle.
  • Use digital tools to fit a trigonometric curve to the graph of average daylight hours per month in a chosen city. Compare the graphs for cities in the Southern hemisphere to those in the Northern hemisphere, or a city close to the equator versus one closer to a pole.
  • Given graphs of sine, cosine and tangent, sketch the graph of their reciprocals.

Further advice is given in support materials which provide teaching strategies, supports and scaffolds demonstrating how to support the diversity of learners in Mathematics 7–10.

system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Trigonometry D (Path)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Key ideas

Students:

  • identify and describe examples of direct and inverse variation
  • identify and describe graphs involving direct and inverse variation
  • solve problems involving direct and inverse variation
  • represent direct variation graphically

Key terms

  • constant    
  • curve                     
  • direct variation
  • gradient     
  • inverse variation
  • linear         
  • proportion                          

Background knowledge

Making connections

ConnectionsOutcome or Stage

When looking at the language of direct variation, a connection can be made to symmetry (if 𝑦 ∝ 𝑥 then 𝑥 ∝ 𝑦) and transitivity (if 𝑦 ∝ 𝑥 and 𝑥 ∝ z then 𝑦 ∝ z).



Stage 5 Linear relationships C

Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 2

Graphs of direct variation connect to linear relationships.

Stage 4 Linear Relationships

Stage 5 Linear Relationships A

Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced

Indirect variation is represented graphically by a hyperbola restricted to positive values of the quantities.

Stage 5 Non-linear relationships C

Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced

Indirect variation is connected to polygons as the exterior angle size of regular polygons is inversely proportional to the number of sides of the regular polygon.Stage 5 Properties of geometrical figures B
Applications of direct variation can be seen in circles as the radius of a circle is directly proportional to the circumference of the circle. The area of a circle is also directly proportional to the square of its radius.Stage 4 Length
In exponential growth and decay the rate of change of a quantity varies directly with the size of the quantity at any instant, and in the modified growth model the rate of change of a quantity varies directly with the difference in the size of the quantity and a fixed quantity at any instant.Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 1
Newton’s second law of motion states the acceleration of a body is proportional to the resultant force that acts on the body and inversely proportional to the mass of the body. In problems involving the motion of a particle moving vertically (upwards or downwards) in a resisting medium and under the influence of gravity, resistance is proportional to the speed of the particle.Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 2
Proportionality is used to describe the relationship between force, mass and acceleration. Explain the relationship between distance, speed and time. Investigate the quantitative features of waves including frequency, wavelength and speed using 𝑉 = 𝑓𝜆 and relate this to musical instruments. Explain the relationship between resistance, voltage and current, using Ohm's Law. The illumination from a source of light is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source.Stage 5 Science
On a map drawn to scale, the distance between any 2 points on the map is proportional to the distance between the 2 locations that the points represent, with the constant of proportionality being the scale of the map.Stage 4, 5 and 6 Geography
Oil price is directly proportional to the number of barrels. The amount of GST payable on an item is directly proportional to the cost of the item. For a given interest rate, the amount of interest earned over a fixed period is directly proportional to the amount invested. Proportionality is used in exchange rates, the cost of an item in euros is proportional to its cost in dollars.Real-world applications

Non-routine problem solving

Further advice is given in support materials which provide teaching strategies, supports and scaffolds demonstrating how to support the diversity of learners in Mathematics 7–10.

title.name: 📜 Title
title.value: Teaching advice for Variation and rates of change A (Path)

system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Variation and rates of change A (Path)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Key ideas

Students:

  • describe the rate of change of a graph as constant or variable, increasing or decreasing
  • interpret distance–time graphs when speed is variable
  • construct graphical representations of rates of change of quantities over time from descriptions

Key terms

  • constant
  • proportion
  • rates
  • variable (algebra)

Background knowledge

  • The relationship between speed, time and distance
  • Gradients of lines in particular contexts
  • Rates as a comparison between two different quantities
  • Using and creating graphs of linear relationships

Making connections

ConnectionsOutcome or Stage
Speed is the rate of change of distance over time.Stage 4 Ratios and Rates
Graphs of direct variation and linear relationships have a constant rate of change.

Stage 4 Linear Relationships

Stage 5 Variation and rates of change A

Variable rates of change are represented by non-linear relationships.Stage 5 Non-linear relationships A & B
Distance–time graphs and equations are used to investigate stopping distance and stopping times.Stage 6 Mathematics Standard 2
Velocity is the rate of change of an object’s position over time.Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced
The rate of change of velocity over time is acceleration and the gradient of a velocity–time graph gives the acceleration.Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced
The rate of change of a quantity over time is given by its derivative with respect to time.

Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced

Stage 6 Mathematics Extension 1

Non-routine problem solving

  • Construct a graph representing the situation where one athlete has a head start on another runner, but the second athlete wins the race. Given the speed and length of the head start, calculate the speed the second athlete must run in order to win a race of a given length.
  • View footage of Usain Bolt’s 100-metre final at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. Draw a distance–time graph to represent the graph. Use terminology such as increasing at an increasing rate or increasing at a decreasing rate.
  • Model, record data and sketch graphs to investigate the distance of a moving object from a fixed point in relation to time. Examine how changing speed and changing direction impact the graph. Record the distance at fixed time intervals so that a graph can be drawn to represent each situation.

Further advice is given in support materials which provide teaching strategies, supports and scaffolds demonstrating how to support the diversity of learners in Mathematics 7–10.

system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Variation and rates of change B (Path)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Key ideas

Students:

  • find the volume of composite prisms made up of cross-sections involving triangles and rectangles
  • find the volume of right prisms with cross-sections in the form of sectors of a circle
  • find the volume of composite solids involving right prisms and cylinders
  • solve practical problems related to the volumes and capacities of right prisms, cylinders and related composite solids

Key terms

  • capacity
  • composite
  • cross-section
  • cylinder
  • quadrant
  • sector
  • uniform
  • volume

Background knowledge

  • Finding volumes of right prisms
  • Finding volumes of cylinders
  • Finding areas of triangles, rectangles, circles and composite shapes
  • Solving multi-step equations
  • Substituting into formulas
  • Finding areas of semicircles, quadrants and sectors
  • Converting between units of volume and capacity

Making connections

ConnectionsOutcome or Stage
Finding volume connects to equations and the ability to solve multi-step equations.Stage 5 Equations
Finding volumes of composite solids connects to using the formula to find the area of circles and sectors to solve problems.Stage 4 Area
Develop and apply the formula for finding the volume of a right prism and cylinder.Stage 4 Volume
Some practical problems will connect to financial mathematics.Stage 5 Financial Mathematics
Students could find the capacity of containers, the density of materials and the amount of a substance needed to fill a mould or cast.Real-world applications
There is a connection to the study of soil profiles, mountain and hill cross-sections and cross-sections on topographic maps using contour lines.Stage 6 Geography
This topic can be connected to the ratio of surface area to volume of cells. Students could investigate: ‘Why are cells so small?’Stage 6 Biology
This topic connects to optimisation problems involving surface area and volume.Stage 6 Mathematics Advanced
There is a connection to measuring ingredients in cooking, modifying and adjusting recipes and selecting appropriately sized vessels for cooking.Real-world applications
Practical problems involving volume.Stage 6 Num CEC 1.3

Non-routine problem solving

  • A rectangular roof that is 15 m long and 6 m wide collects rainwater and directs it into a cylindrical water tank. The water tank is 1.2 m in diameter and is 2.4 m high. If 25 mm of rain falls, how far up the water tank will the water level reach?
  • The water cooler at work holds 15 L of water. A cylindrical glass measures 8 cm in diameter and is 15 cm high. How many glasses of water can be completely filled from a full water cooler?
  • Consider 2 cylinders where one cylinder is twice as wide but only half as high as the other cylinder. Do these cylinders have the same volume?
  • A cylindrical can is to hold 375 mL of drink. Which dimensions of the can would have the minimum surface area? How does this compare to 375 mL cans we find in supermarkets?

Further advice is given in support materials which provide teaching strategies, supports and scaffolds demonstrating how to support the diversity of learners in Mathematics 7–10.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

In Stage 1, students develop a range of strategies using recall of number bonds to make 10 and solve addition and subtraction problems. An understanding of the meaning of the equality sign (=) is considered the basis of relational thinking in algebra. When thinking relationally about the equality symbol, students consider the number sentence as a whole, before analysing the component parts and the operations involved. This interpretation sets students up for success in algebra.

Teaching advice

Understanding place value

Calculating with multi-digit numbers does not need to wait until students have fully mastered place value. It typically takes years before students are able to integrate the different aspects of place value. Research confirms (National Research Council 2001) that students can develop an understanding of both the base-ten system and procedures for calculating when they have opportunities to explore how and why the procedures work.

Encourage students to explain their strategies in solving addition and subtraction problems and to develop ways of recording their actions. Discuss the merits of various strategies in terms of how practical and efficient they are.

Recording mental strategies using an empty number line

Using structured quantitative models like bead strings or linking cubes can help students see how addition and subtraction of numbers can be recorded. When using bead strings, it is important that students are familiar with the way that colour is used on the bead string to show groups of 5. When students are familiar with the structure of these models, combining and separating quantities can be linked to recording on an empty number line. Below, the bead string is repeated as 5 red bead strings, followed by 5 white bead strings.

Activity: Forming 8 and 5.

Activity: Combining 8 and 5, aligned to an empty number line.

Jump strategy on a number line

In this addition or subtraction strategy the student places the first number on an empty number line. They then move forwards or backwards to perform the calculation, often first by tens and then by ones. Encourage students to make use of multiples of 10 and number bonds. These require fewer jumps and are more efficient.

An example of using the jump strategy method for addition: 46 + 33

An example of using the jump strategy method for subtraction: 79 – 33

Separate 10s and 1s

In this strategy, sometimes called a split strategy, the student separates the tens from the ones (units). Each is added separately and then combined to find the final answer.

A common error when this method is used for subtraction questions is the smaller from larger error. For example, separating the tens in 96 – 58 results in 90 – 50. Some students may then swap the order for the units 8 – 6. This produces an incorrect answer of 42. For this reason, the split strategy should only be used for addition.

Inverse strategy

An inverse operation reverses the effect of the original operation. The shopkeeper’s method of giving change uses the inverse strategy of addition to perform a subtraction. Because addition and subtraction are inverse operations a student can add up from the smaller number to the larger number to obtain the answer. 

For example, using the inverse strategy to solve 65 – 37 would proceed as follows:

  • Start at 37
  • Add 3 to make 40
  • Then add 20 to make 60
  • Finally add 5 to make 65
  • And so the answer is 3 + 20 + 5 = 28

Equality

Students need to understand the different uses for the equality sign (=). Many students interpret = as a signal to perform an operation.

For example, when read aloud, 4 + 1 = 5 is often stated as four plus one equals five. While this is consistent with left-to-right decoding when reading text, it does not promote an understanding of the relational nature of the equality sign.

Students need to:

  • interpret the equal sign relationally
  • recognise that the two sides can be exchanged.

To assist students in understanding the equality sign (=), teachers can:

  • vary how number sentences are recorded
  • read the relational symbol as is the same amount as.

The number sentence 5 = 4 + 1 is also a valid statement of equality. Five is the same amount as four plus one.

Gesturing

Gesturing when teaching can help students appreciate the two sides in an equality relationship. For example:

I want to make one side [sweeping left hand back and forth under the left side of the problem] equal to the other side [sweeping right hand back and forth under the right side of the problem].

This can encourage students to produce similar gestures, which can aid learning.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following questions can be used to determine if a student can reason about the relationship between addition and subtraction to solve problems involving partitioning.

Bridging to the next multiple of 10

By the end of Stage 1, students should typically be able to use their knowledge of number bonds of ten to solve addition and subtraction problems such as:

  • I have $23. How much more do I need to have $30?
  • I have $34. How much more do I need to have $40?

Knowledge of number bonds (for example combinations of ten) as known facts is only useful when students can apply this knowledge to solve other tasks.

Bridging through the next multiple of 10

By the end of Stage 1, students should typically be able to bridge to 10 to solve two-digit addition and subtraction problems, such as:

  • I have $44. How much more do I need to have $51? How did you work it out?
  • I have $25. How much more do I need to have $32? How did you work it out?

Students should use number bonds up to ten to solve addition and subtraction problems. Number bonds forming seven (eg 6 and 1) assist in solving 44 + _ = 51. Similarly, number bonds forming seven (eg 5 and 2) can assist in solving 25 + _ = 32.

Bridging to the next multiple of ten and bridging through the next multiple of ten are foundational combining and partitioning strategies. Revisit these strategies regularly for consolidation.

Students should develop these flexible strategies when dealing with one-digit and two-digit number problems before exposure to two-digit and two-digit addition/subtraction problems (where the difference is greater than 20).

While the context of money has been used, teachers can adapt these questions and change the context. The difference between the values in the following questions is more than five to discourage counting on.

Reasoning about quantity linking addition and subtraction

The following questions are designed to investigate students’ reasoning about the relation between addition and subtraction. This type of reasoning underpins compensation and estimation methods. It continues to develop in Stage 2. The questions are intended for use after students have had an opportunity to learn the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction.

Strategies and questions

Addition to related subtraction: Can you use this: 27 + 13 = 40 [display the number sentence] to work out 40 – 13 [display the question]?

Subtraction to related addition: Can you use this: 52 – 14 = 38 [display the number sentence] to work out 38 + 14 [display the question]?

Complement principle: If 24 – 7 = 17 [display the number sentence] what is 24 – 17?

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Addition and subtraction typically progress from counting, combining and separating perceptual objects to using numbers as replacements for completed counts.

Teaching advice

Students in Stage 1 can use concrete materials and drawings:

  • to model and solve problems
  • for exploration
  • for concept building.

The recording students make in combining and separating quantities can also provide support for their mental strategies by reducing the load on working memory.

Advanced count-by-ones methods

The first advanced count-by-ones strategies students use for addition and subtraction are counting on and counting back. That is, students:

  • count on from the larger number to find the total of two numbers
  • count back from a number to find the quantity remaining
  • count on or back to find the difference between two numbers.

As outlined briefly in the teaching advice for Early Stage 1, subtraction covers two different situations. Subtraction can involve:

  • taking away from a group, or
  • comparison (determining how many more or fewer when comparing two groups).

Counting on or back

In performing a comparison subtraction, students could use counting on or back from one number to find the difference. This type of subtraction can be more difficult for students to grasp than the taking away type. However, counting on or back can be an efficient method of solving comparison problems when using larger numbers.

Once students are confident with the taking away type, encourage them to use counting on or back where the differences are small (less than five). For example, when comparing 19 with 17, it is easier to count on from 17 than take away 17 objects from a collection of 19.

Using number bonds

Number bonds are pairs of numbers that bond through addition to form another number. Number pairs that bond to form 10 are particularly useful when adding or subtracting. However, students may know number bonds but not use them to add and subtract.

Flexible strategies

Using flexible strategies refers to methods that do not rely on counting by one. Flexible strategies include using known number combinations and bridging to 10, as well as methods of adjusting the numbers in the question without changing the result (sometimes called compensation).

Students who can recall number bonds may still rely on strategies like counting on to solve problems. This is why it is important to model the use of number bonds in addition and subtraction problems.

Bridging to 10

Teachers can begin to model the use of number bonds in bridging to 10 once students are familiar with the number bonds.

For example, 28 + 7 is the same as 28 + 2 + 5 (partitioning the 7 into 2 plus 5 to bridge to the next multiple of ten). This uses the number bond 8 + 2 = 10 as well as partitioning 7.

It is important to explicitly model the use of number bonds in bridging to 10. Many students do not use the number bonds they know to add and subtract (Graven and Venkat 2021).

Quantity value

As well as number bonds, students’ informal mental calculation strategies with two-digit numbers substantially rely on quantity values. Quantity value involves using the value of the parts in a standard partition of a number greater than 10 separately (eg 43 as 40 and 3).

Mental calculation strategies treat the digits in the tens or hundreds column as a quantity in their own right. The 4 in 345 is forty rather than a four in the tens column (or even four tens). Place value has many aspects. The former is the quantity value aspect of place value and the latter the column value aspect.

Language

Difference

In everyday language, the word difference can refer to any attribute. However, it has a specific meaning in number questions, where it means the distance between two numbers on a number line.

Students should develop an understanding that the process of subtraction can be indicated by a variety of language structures. The language used in the comparison type of subtraction can be different from that used in the take away type. For example, how might a teacher say ‘9 minus 3’?

Comparison languageTake away language
What is 3 subtracted from 9?Reduce 9 by 3.
By how much does 9 exceed 3?From 9 take 3.
What number is 3 less than 9?Take 3 from 9.
What is the difference between 9 and 3?9 take away 3.
How many added to 3 make 9?Decrease 9 by 3.
How many more than 3 is 9?From 9 subtract 3.

The many different ways of expressing ‘9 minus 3’ highlights the futility of trying to teach a key word approach to interpreting mathematics questions.

Left

The word ‘left’ can be confusing for students. For example:

  • There were five children in the room. Three went to lunch. How many were left?

Words with the same spelling but different meanings (homographs) are particularly challenging for students learning English as an additional language or dialect.

Word order

It is not simply the vocabulary used in mathematics that can make questions challenging. Word order is crucial. Consider the following two questions:

  • Four is half of what number? (8)
  • What number is half of four? (2)

These two questions use exactly the same words but ask for entirely different responses.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • counting on/counting back
  • combine/plus/add
  • take away/minus
  • the difference between
  • total
  • increase/decrease
  • more than/less than
  • bridge
  • number bond
  • double
  • equals/is equal to/is the same as
  • number sentence
  • strategy.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to investigate if a student can use the cardinal value of numbers in calculating.

A teacher might present the following scenario:

  • I have 13 cards and Kim gave me some more. Altogether, I now have 16 cards.

The teacher could then ask:

  • How many cards did Kim give me?

A student is using the cardinal value of a number like 13 when there is no need to count from 1 to form 13. Recognising that 16 is 3 more (counts) makes use of the additive property. Each counting number represents a part–whole relation.

title.value: Teaching advice for Combining and separating quantities A

system.name: MS S1 Teaching advice for Combining and separating quantities A

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Place value is an important and fundamental concept in early number work. An appreciation of the structure of tens and hundreds forms the foundation for operating with two-digit and three-digit numbers. The focus of representing whole numbers in Stage 1 is developing a robust understanding of the composite units of 10 and 100 that make up two-digit and three-digit numbers.

Teaching advice

Place value

Rather than describing a single property (such as positional value) our place value system has a number of different properties (Ross 2002) or aspects. This includes the following properties:

  • Additive property: The quantity represented by the whole numeral is the sum of the values represented by the individual digits.
  • Positional property: The quantities represented by the individual digits are determined by the position that they hold in the whole numeral.
  • Base-ten property: The values of the positions increase in powers of ten from right to left.
  • Multiplicative property: The value of an individual digit is found by multiplying the face value of the digit by the value assigned to its position.

An understanding of place value numeration develops over time and may include an understanding of:

  • tens and ones
  • regrouping and renaming
  • decimal representation.

Place value understanding needs to be explicitly developed in a range of contexts involving operating with numbers.

Working with two-digit and three-digit numbers

A unit of ten things is considered to be a composite unit if it can be interpreted as both one 10 (a single unit) and ten individual units at the same time.

The focus of representing whole numbers in Stage 1 is developing a robust understanding of the composite units of 10 and 100 that make up two-digit and three-digit numbers.

Using number charts

There are many ways that number charts can be used to support student understanding of the base-ten numeration system (Bay-Williams and Fletcher 2017). Number charts either start at 0 or 1 and can provide opportunities for students to notice:

  • ten as 10 ones and 1 ten
  • one hundred as 10 tens
  • patterns, such as 10 more.

Modern number charts often do not stop at 100 but continue to 120. This provides opportunities for students to recognise how the counting pattern continues beyond 100. Some charts also start at the bottom and build up, to model how the process of adding makes higher totals (going up the chart).

Identifying the nearest multiple of ten

Many procedures used when rounding numbers emphasise the digit values more than the units of ten and hundred, eg rounding up if the last digit is five or more.

Instead of teaching procedures for rounding to the nearest 10 or 100, place the emphasis on:

  • developing the quantity value of numbers
  • identifying the nearest ten (or hundred) to a number.

Using Number talks to assess student reasoning

Number talks (Parrish 2011) are brief discussions that focus on how students solve a problem in their heads. They encourage students to communicate their reasoning. Number talks may be useful in assessing students’ understanding to reason about representations of whole numbers to 1000.

When using number talks, it is important to ensure all students can participate. Incremental strategies such as think-pair-share can be effective. Students learning English as an additional language or dialect, including Aboriginal students, can be supported by using home-language buddies to engage in the number talks. Students from a range of cultural backgrounds may be more comfortable sharing their thinking as part of a pair or small group, rather than individually. Some students with disability communicate through a variety of verbal or nonverbal communication systems or techniques. The problems used in a number talk should have more than one method of finding the answer.

Number talks that use the principles of a yarning circle or mathematical journals can provide opportunities to engage with mathematical storytelling. Students share their solutions, while the teacher models recording their thinking. Students should be provided with opportunities to engage with mathematics using storytelling, such as recounting a method or strategy used to solve a problem.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to investigate if a student’s understanding of the positional value of the digits aligns with the cardinal value of the numeral.

Digit-correspondence task: 16 tiles

The following is an example of a digit-correspondence task – a style of question frequently used by Ross (2002), a researcher in children’s numerical thinking.

Ask the student to count a number of items, typically between 10 and 40, and write or identify the numeral corresponding to the total. The student is then asked to show with the items how the digits in the recorded number represent the total.

S: [Writes 16.]

T: So that number is?

S: Sixteen.

T: And there are how many here? [Points to the 16 tiles.]

S: Sixteen.

T: OK. So with the number 16 … this 6 here [points to the 6 in the 16] can you show me with the tiles how you would make that?

S: [Makes 6 tiles as 3 and 3.] Three and three.

T: Let’s put them on the 6 side.

S: [Moves the tiles to the right of the digit 6.]

T: Great. And this 1 here [points to the 1 in 16] … what would that mean for the tiles?

S: For the units [moves one tile next to the 1] … it stands for the units in the tens and ones.

T: Tens and ones. Ok. Is this 1 here [points to the 1 in 16] does that mean a unit or something else?

S: A unit.

T: [Revoices.] A unit. So altogether [points to the 7 tiles on the paper near the written 16 and circles them in the air] there are how many here?

S: Seven.

T: [Revoices.] Seven. Now if there are 7 here and this number is 16 and there are 16 tiles altogether, what happens to these tiles? [Points to the remaining 9 tiles.]

S: They are the leftovers.

This student’s understanding of the positional value of the digits does not align with the cardinal value of the numeral.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Addition and subtraction develop from students counting, combining and separating objects. In time, they learn to use number words or numerals as replacements for completed counts.

The processes of addition and subtraction are developed together to provide the foundation for the understanding of their inverse relationship. Reasoning about the way numbers can be combined and separated supports understanding the actions of adding and subtracting as inverse operations.

Teaching advice

While addition covers combining two or more groups, subtraction covers two different situations:

  • taking away from a group
  • comparing two groups.

Students should first be able to compare groups of objects by matching, using one-to-one correspondence. They then determine how many more or how many fewer objects there are in a group.

Students need many experiences that require them to relate their knowledge to the vocabulary and conceptual frameworks of mathematics. Visualising, modelling, drawing and writing mathematical problems can provide these experiences when combining and separating quantities.

Storytelling is an effective way for students to conceptualise and communicate mathematical ideas, such as combining and separating quantities, and assists students to recognise the purposeful nature of mathematics in real-world contexts. Mathematics as storytelling (Matthews 2008) can support the engagement and achievement of Aboriginal students, and all students.

Formal writing of number sentences, including the use of the symbols +, − and =, is introduced in Stage 1.

Reasoning about number relations

Reasoning about number relations involves students being able to discuss how addition and subtraction are related and how they are different. Reasoning in this case involves appreciating why addition and subtraction are inverse or ‘opposite’ operations.

Reasoning about inverse relationships

Students reason about number relations when modelling addition and subtraction through gestures and/or words as they combine and separate groups of items. Students notice that if they have ten items, they can separate the items into two piles, say four and six, then combine them again, and still have ten items. Students might also notice that they can remove four items from the pile of ten and have six (subtraction), then move the four back to have ten (addition). These actions, combining and separating, are ‘opposite’ to each other.

Reasoning about number relationships

Students may know that 5 + 4 and 4 + 5 are ‘turn around facts’ but may not be able to give reasons why they result in the same total. Modelling what these number relations look like assists in building the generalisation that it does not matter which order you add the numbers, the total is still the same (the commutative property of addition).

Building reasoning also needs to include opportunities to reflect on how this process is not true for subtraction. Understanding that we cannot change the order of numbers for subtraction is an important concept. Investigating what happens when you have three items and try to take away five items, and there not being enough items to complete the task, is an important step in reasoning about number relations.

Relations and relationships

The syllabus refers to students establishing number relations and also working with relationships between numbers. The terms ‘relation’ and ‘relationship’ have very similar meanings when used as nouns. ‘Relation’ means the manner in which two things may be associated. ‘Relationship’ means connection or association. For example, there is a relation between the numbers 3, 5 and 8, and their relationship is additive.

Some Aboriginal students may have well-developed conceptual understandings of quantitative ‘relations’ and ‘relationships’ based on cultural knowledge and practices, such as connections within Country, kinship systems or community structures.

Language

Some students may need assistance when two tenses are used in the one problem. For example, I had six beans and took away four. How many do I have now?

Students may be supported by the provision of a real-world context or story to clarify the use of past and present tense. For example, I had six beans and my brother took away four to give to our cousins. How many do I have now?

Questions involving comparison subtraction (how many more?) are much more difficult than determining which is more? Students may just state the higher number when asked how many more. In part, students find comparison subtraction difficult because they are not familiar with the question type. Comparison subtraction requires students to determine the difference between two quantities.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate: 

  • count forwards
  • combines with
  • joins
  • count backwards
  • take away
  • how many more
  • altogether
  • makes.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to investigate if a student can reason about number relations by combining and separating or comparing collections of objects. Note that the number of counters may need to be adjusted for students with a lower counting range.

Present the student with a pile of 15 counters or similar objects. For some students visual images or assistive technology may be required.

Ask the student:

Can you get me 8 counters from the pile? How do you know that is 8?

Are there more counters here [point at the 8 counters] or more counters there [point at the 7 remaining]? How do you know?

If you put them all together, how many are there?

Typical development by the end of Early Stage 1 would be for students to be able to count (with one-to-one correspondence) to determine a total within the range of 1 to 20.

content.value:
Why is it important?

The process of sharing objects equally and putting shared objects back together to form one collection develops students’ understanding of the link between multiplication and division and provides the foundation for a conceptual understanding of their inverse relationship. In Early Stage 1, students develop strategies for forming groups based on the structure and pattern of numbers as countable units. Strategies related to forming groups in the early years are foundational to the multiplicative structure of number (Mendes and Ferreira 2008).

Reasoning about patterns

In Early Stage 1, reasoning about relations between pattern units involves recognising the pattern unit and being able to continue the pattern (Samara and Clements 2009). Starting with two-part patterns AB, students should be encouraged to extend, correct and create patterns. Once students can recognise a two-part pattern, they should learn to fill in missing elements in a pattern, and then copy and extend a pattern. In forming groups in Early Stage 1, students learn to connect the processes of patterning within number. This is foundational knowledge for learning algebra in later stages.

Teaching advice

Forming groups should, wherever possible, engage students in manipulating concrete materials. Alternatively, visual or digital forms of modelling groups may be used by students with complex learning needs. The emphasis is on modelling groups of the same size and describing them.

Students initially distribute objects one by one until the supply is exhausted. Teachers should draw attention to the number of groups and the number in each group. After students have shared objects equally, the process can be reversed, putting the shared objects back together to form one collection.

There are two processes associated with forming groups. The first looks at sharing when students know the number of groups. The second involves finding the number of groups when you know how many are in each group.

ProcessTypeDescriptionExample
Equal sharingPartitiveDistributing items one at a time into a set number of groups.A student has a number of pop sticks and three cups. They share out the pop sticks into the cups one at a time.
Equal groupingQuotitiveDistributing the same number of items into an unknown number of groups.A student has 12 pop sticks and wants to make groups of four. They place four pop sticks down, then another four, and so on.

Forming groups of objects that have the same number of elements helps students develop the mathematical concept of equality.

Students who have already demonstrated forming equal groups by sharing and counting collections of objects could be extended in their learning by:

  • posing problems or questions that can be solved by forming groups
  • using their understanding of forming equal groups to represent a number in different ways, for example 12 as 3 groups of 4, 4 groups of 3, 6 groups of 2, or 2 groups of 6.

Using familiar objects to represent equal groups and patterns can be useful in supporting student understanding of these concepts. It is important to keep in mind that students come from diverse backgrounds and experiences, and objects that are considered to be familiar to one student may not be familiar to another.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate: 

  • group
  • share
  • equal
  • pattern
  • repeat.

Check that students are familiar with groups of two like things being called pairs.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to investigate if a student can form equal groups by sharing and counting collections of objects.

Provide the student with a pile of at least 20 linking cubes or similar objects.

Ask:

Can you make 5 towers, with 3 blocks in each tower?

How many towers do you have?

How many in each tower?

How many altogether?

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Manipulation of a variety of real objects and shapes is crucial to the development of appropriate levels of visualisation, language and representation. Also, measuring the areas of objects using informal units enables students to develop some key understandings of measurement. These include:

  • repeatedly placing units so that there are no gaps or overlaps
  • understanding that the units must be equal in size.

Teaching advice

2D shape

Representing and visualising three-dimensional objects and two-dimensional shapes are developing in Stage 1 and should be fostered through practical activities and communication.

Students should be able to recognise shapes presented in different orientations.

Students should have experiences identifying both regular shapes (all sides and angles equal) and irregular shapes. It is not expected that students understand or distinguish between regular and irregular shapes in Stage 1.

Area

Area relates to the measurement of two-dimensional space, in the same way that volume relates to the measurement of three-dimensional space. The attribute of area is the amount of surface (either flat or curved) and can be measured in square units:

  • square centimetres (cm2)
  • square metres (m2).

Informal units

Measuring the areas of objects using informal units enables students to develop some key understandings of measurement. These include:

  • repeatedly placing units so that there are no gaps or overlaps
  • understanding that the units must be equal in size.

Covering surfaces with a range of informal units should assist students in understanding that some units tessellate (fit together without gaps or overlaps) and are therefore more suitable for measuring area.

When students draw the covering of a rectangle with unit squares, some will draw each individual square while others will draw a combination of individual squares and lines. Some students will draw lines to represent rows and then mark off squares individually while others will draw an array using lines.

Grid structure

Students should be encouraged to make, draw and describe the spatial structure (grid) for rectangular shapes. To assist students in noticing the grid structure, outline cardboard square tiles.

Students should develop procedures for counting tile or grid units so that no units are missed or counted twice. They should be encouraged to identify and use efficient strategies for counting, eg using repeated addition or skip counting.

It is important that:

  • students have had some measurement experiences including cutting up and rearranging areas before being asked to estimate areas
  • a variety of estimation strategies is taught.

Language

2D shape

The term ‘vertex’ (plural: ‘vertices’) refers to the point where:

  • two straight sides of a two-dimensional shape meet
  • three or more faces of a three-dimensional object meet.

The term ‘shape’ refers to a two-dimensional figure. The term ‘object’ refers to a three-dimensional figure.

Students learn to identify a number of different polygons including:

  • triangles
  • quadrilaterals
  • pentagons
  • hexagons
  • octagons.

The names of these shapes reflect Latin and Greek influences:

  • Triangle: from the Latin triangulus, meaning three angles or corners. It is helpful to check if students know any other words where ‘tri’ also means three, such as tricycle or triceratops.
  • Quadrilateral: from the Latin quadrilaterus, meaning four sides or flanks. While squares and rectangles are examples of quadrilaterals, a square is also a special type of rectangle.
  • Polygon: comes from ancient Greek (written in the Latin alphabet) and means many angles. Pentagons (five angles), hexagons (six angles) and octagons (eight angles) are all examples of polygons.

A shape has line symmetry if matching parts are produced when it is folded along a line of symmetry. Each part represents the mirror image of the other.

Vocabulary

2D shape

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • shape
  • circle
  • triangle
  • quadrilateral
  • square
  • rectangle
  • pentagon
  • hexagon
  • octagon
  • orientation
  • features
  • side
  • vertex (vertices)
  • shape
  • symmetry
  • slide
  • reflection.

Area

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • area
  • cover
  • surface
  • measure
  • row/column
  • grid
  • gap
  • overlap
  • unit
  • estimate.

content.value:
Why is it important?

Representing numbers in a variety of ways is essential for developing number sense.

Students can represent numbers using:

Representation typeExample
Number wordsfive
Numerals5
Finger patterns
Collections of perceptual items5 pencils

As a student learns to represent whole numbers, they begin to move between the number words used in counting, numerals and quantity. Students could use concrete materials, gestures (such as nodding) or body tallying (Butterworth 1999) to indicate the count. A student should be able to select a given number of items (more than five) from a larger collection if the number is represented by a word or symbol. For example, a student is shown the numeral 8, and counts out eight items from a collection of twenty items.

The cardinality principle recognises that the last number name represents the total number in the collection. This principle marks a profound conceptual achievement, understanding how counting works (Paliwal and Baroody 2018).

Teaching advice

Counting

Counting is an important component of number knowledge and the early learning of operations. In Early Stage 1, typical development would be for students to be able to count to 30 and elaborate the count by stating the next number without restarting the count.

Counting develops over time as number words are assigned progressively more sophisticated meanings. The process of learning to count, which starts with memorising a few words of the counting list and continues to the point of understanding the cardinality principle, is the process by which students develop their first mental representations of exact, larger numerical quantities (as high as they can count) (Sarnecka et al. 2015).

Counting with understanding

Counting with understanding involves:

  • counting with one-to-one correspondence (one-to-one principle)
  • recognising that the last number name represents the total number in the collection (cardinal principle).

Other counting principles include:

  • stable-order principle: you always say number words in a particular sequence when counting
  • order-irrelevance principle: the order in which you count items does not change the total counted
  • abstraction principle: it does not matter what you count, numbers can be used to count anything and the process for counting is always the same.

There is a distinction between counting by rote and counting with understanding. A student might produce the correct sequence of number words to 15. The same student may not understand the one-to-one correspondence between the number words and the number of objects. It is important to assess one-to-one correspondence and cardinality within a student’s counting range.

When students are learning to count, they can often produce a higher rote count than the largest collection they can count to with understanding. This is why the rote count expectation is at least 30, while students are expected to only represent numbers to at least 20.

Explicit modelling and multiple opportunities for guided and independent practice can support the development of the cardinality principle. Counting a set of objects followed by emphasising the last word counted, and then repeating the final word in the count while gesturing to the corresponding objects can support this understanding (Paliwal and Baroody 2018).

Distinguishing between teens and multiples of ten

The teen numbers in English are often the most difficult for students. The oral language of teen numbers is the reverse of the usual pattern of 'tens first and then ones'.

Students should learn to distinguish between commonly confused similar-sounding numerals, such as 13 and 30 or 15 and 50. Phonemic awareness can assist students in moving between numerals and number words (Lopes-Silva et al. 2014).

Although students in Early Stage 1 are not expected to count sequentially beyond 30, many students may be able to count by tens (10, 20, 30, 40, 50 …). It is important to make the distinction between the suffixes teen and ty as early as possible to reduce the risk of confusing number names when counting higher.

Subitising

The word 'subitise' is derived from Latin and means 'to arrive suddenly'. Subitising is immediately recognising the number of objects in a small (up to four) random collection without having to count the objects. For up to four items, response times increase by about 40–100 ms for every dot, while for larger numbers they increase by 250–350 ms per dot, leading to a clear change in the slope of the response curve (Mandler and Shebo 1982).

It enables us to use grouping structures when establishing the number of items in larger collections.

Perceptual subitising has two different forms:

  • preverbal subitising – does not require naming the number of objects. For example, infants are thought to use preverbal subitising to distinguish between magnitudes, before they learn to speak (Tan and Bryant 2000).
  • verbal subitising – number words express quantity.

Pattern recognition, sometimes referred to as ‘conceptual subitising’ (Clements, 1999), can assist students to develop capabilities of recognising units and combining numbers.

We can also recognise larger numbers of dots when presented in a known pattern (such as the figure below). Many students may initially see this as groups of three.

Figure 1: A collection of dots in a known pattern.

To support the development of subitising, students should develop an understanding that quantities have names. Students should understand that number words have useful purposes for counting and for comparisons (Staves 2019). 

Students who have already demonstrated the cardinality principle and subitising could be extended in their learning by focusing on the pattern structure of numbers through dice and domino patterns and through representing quantities to 20.

Language

The oral count starts as a fixed recitation of number words. It then progresses through overlapping phases of acquiring and elaborating the counting sequence. In the elaboration phase, students learn to continue the count from any point, identifying the number word that comes before or after any counting word.

The challenges of learning the teen number words in English mean that students can often identify which number word comes before twenty-three, in advance of identifying the number word before thirteen.

Languages other than English often have different patterns for number words. Acknowledging the structure of number words in students’ home language will be important in supporting students to understand representations of number in English. Explicit teaching of patterns of number words in English, paired with verbal and visual representations, can assist.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate: 

  • count forwards
  • count backwards
  • number after/number before
  • one less/one more
  • zero
  • number words
  • numerals
  • is the same
  • count
  • pattern
  • ones
  • coins.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to investigate if a student can read and represent whole numbers to at least 20.

  • Provide the student with a shuffled set of number cards (1 to 20).
  • Ask the student to put the numbers in order from smallest to largest. For some students, ordering the cards may include gesture, eye gaze, or verbally telling the teacher.

If the student is unsuccessful, ask the student to count for you. Have the student start from one or two numbers before the initial error in ordering the cards.

If the student is successful, indicate different cards and ask, What number is that?

How the student responds to these questions will provide information on which numerals (1 to 20) they can identify. You could assess numeral recognition by asking the student to indicate various numbers as you say them.

For students with diverse needs this task could be adapted for determining numeral recognition, identification and meaning. This could be done using matching activities, where students are presented with a sample (for example the numeral 5) and a number of pictures to select from (including one correct image). Start with one or two incorrect pictures, increasing as the student becomes proficient. Incorrect pictures could include blank cards, images of larger or smaller quantities and then numbers.

To check if a student demonstrates an understanding of how whole numbers indicate quantity, cover over the first five cards. Ask the student:

How many numbers have I covered up?

[Prompt, if needed] Look at the numbers that are left.

How do you know?

Does the student need to count from one to determine how many are covered? Or does the student recognise that if 6 is visible, 1 to 5 are covered?

Reasoning that five cards have been covered, based on what remains uncovered, suggests an understanding of how whole numbers indicate quantity.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Teachers should encourage students to develop efficient grouping strategies when counting large collections. For example, they can count out groups of five or ten and then find the total using the groups. Grouping makes it easier to check the total.

By combining quantities in a variety of ways, students can learn there are more efficient ways to total large collections than counting one by one.

Teaching advice

A unit of ten things is considered to be a composite unit if it can be interpreted as both one 10 (a single unit) and ten individual units at the same time.

Numeral zero

The numeral 0 plays two separate roles in reading numbers:

  • a lexical tag on the end of a number generating its name, eg 20, 100
  • internal zeros used as place holders, eg 107.

The number line

The number line can be a powerful model for thinking about quantities. To be most effective, the number line needs to be introduced when students can make use of its defining feature – length.

When numeral cards are placed in order side by side they form a numeral track. A numeral track is an ordered sequence of whole numbers. It acts as a counting model because the numerals in the track support counting.

The number line is a more sophisticated model of number. It introduces the idea of distance between numbers. The number line is a model of length. With a number line, students have to count the length units and not the numerals.

Figure 4: An example of a number line (0–9) with a length of 5 shown from zero to 5.

In Geometric measure, students are encouraged to make a measuring device with uniform units before using a ruler. A similar approach can be used to introduce the number line.

Students need both knowledge of numerals and the quantities they represent to use number lines.

Language

In Australia, the word and is used when reading a number greater than 100 or writing it in words.

For example, five hundred and sixty-three.

Students should be made aware that when numbers are used as labels they are said differently. For example:

  • bus numbers
  • postcodes
  • telephone numbers.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • count forwards/count backwards
  • number before/number after
  • more than/less than
  • number line/numeral track
  • digit
  • zero
  • tens/groups of ten
  • round to
  • counters
  • coins
  • dollars/cents
  • odd/even.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

Acquiring an understanding of whole numbers does not develop uniformly. As well as learning the sequence of number names for multiples of 10 to successfully cross the decades, students need experience with the sequence beyond 100.

It is not unusual for students to be uncertain of what number follows 109 (Gould 2017). Teachers may use the following strategies to determine if a student can identify the repeating pattern of counting numbers beyond 100.

  • Ask the student: What number comes after 109?
  • Alternatively, ask the student to: Start counting from 106 and stop at 120.

As students need to learn how to represent numbers using numerals, you could also ask them to record the number that comes after 109. Answers like ‘10010’ for one hundred and ten are attempts at literal transcoding.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Developing and retaining mental images of objects is an important skill for students. Manipulation of a variety of real three-dimensional geometric objects and two-dimensional shapes supports the development of relevant mathematical language and representation. Opportunities for these kinds of activities occur in the classroom, the playground and outside the school. Investigating the type of three-dimensional objects that are stackable makes use of the features of geometric objects in quantifying volume.

Teaching advice

Volume

The attribute of volume is the amount of space occupied by an object. Students in Stage 1 need experience in constructing volumes using informal units such as cubic blocks. Volume is formally measured in later stages using cubic units, such as:

  • cubic centimetres (cm3)
  • cubic metres (m3).

Internal volume (capacity)

Internal volume (capacity) refers to the amount a container can hold and is only used in relation to containers. It generally refers to liquid measurement, that is, the amount of liquid is equal to the internal volume of a container. Students in Stage 1 need experience in filling containers with: 

  • continuous materials such as water
  • discrete objects such as marbles.

Internal volume is formally measured in later stages using units, such as:

  • millilitres (mL)
  • litres (L).

Language

3D objects

The terms used to describe the dimensions of three-dimensional objects take different forms. Although ‘length’, ‘width’ and ‘height’ are commonly used for the three dimensions, the term ‘depth’ is sometimes used in place of height, particularly when referring to an internal dimension.

In everyday use, the context guides our choice of terms:

  • the ‘length’ of a piece of string
  • the ‘width’ of a doorway
  • the ‘height’ of a building
  • the ‘depth’ of a pool.

However, in describing an object that can readily change its orientation such as a wooden block, the choice of labels is not fixed. What would be described as the ‘height’ of the block will depend on how it is positioned.

The terms ‘length’, ‘width’ and ‘height’ can be introduced when students are engaged in using rectangular prisms.

In geometry, the term ‘face’ refers to a flat surface with only straight edges, as in prisms and pyramids. For example, a cube has six faces.

Curved surfaces, such as those found in cones, cylinders and spheres, are not classified as faces. Similarly, flat surfaces with curved boundaries, such as the circular surfaces of cones and cylinders, are not faces.

Internal volume (capacity)

When working with students in Stage 1 it is recommended that the terms ‘capacity’ and ‘internal volume’ be used interchangeably.

The internal volume of a closed container will be slightly less than its volume. Internal volume is based on the inside dimensions, while volume is determined by the outside dimensions of the container.

It is not necessary to refer to these definitions with students as capacity is not taught as a concept separate from volume until Stage 4.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • object
  • cube
  • cylinder
  • sphere
  • flat/curved surface
  • face
  • edge
  • prism
  • internal volume/capacity
  • has more/has less
  • measure.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Describing the data and its spread, as well as creating data displays, draws upon students’ skills in quantitative and spatial reasoning. Comparing probabilities relies on and can support the development of proportional reasoning. When students need to reason beyond the available data, the ideas of chance or likelihood are introduced. Further, comparing probabilities relies on proportional reasoning.

Teaching advice

In Early Stage 1, students collect information about themselves and their environment with teacher assistance. They use objects as data and group these objects into a data display. Objects should be grouped according to characteristics, such as colour, size, shape or texture. Students begin to reason about relations by applying their counting knowledge and skills in comparing the size of different groups of objects.

As students learn to predict responses to and respond to questions about information collected, they begin to develop an introductory understanding of probability. Probability can be a rather challenging concept to grasp as the outcome of many events cannot be predicted with total certainty. Developing a widely acceptable definition of probability took nearly three centuries and was marked by much controversy. In simple terms, probability is how likely something is to happen.

Probability can appear to work against our sense of balance. If a coin has landed heads five times in a row, we expect it to be more likely to turn up tails on the next throw. The idea that what has happened in the past has no impact on the future is challenging for students to understand at this stage of learning. The understanding of chance situations is developed through the use of simple experiments which produce data so that students can make comparisons. However, students’ personal beliefs, such as favourite colours, influence their predictions of chance events. In Early Stage 1, some chance experiments may be included as part of an investigation that collects data.

Students will need support in understanding the key vocabulary demands associated with probability, provided below.

Language

The language of chance is introduced in Early Stage 1 through discussions of data collected. Discussing possible outcomes of data collections can help clarify events that are certain and those that are not.

Question starters include:

  • Could it be …?
  • Why couldn’t it be …?

Using events that are familiar to students will support their understanding of events that are certain and events that are not certain.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • information
  • collect
  • group
  • display
  • objects.
