content.value:
Why is it important?

Learning about position is important in locating one’s self and others in space. The words used in describing position are the basis of the prepositions in English, such as ‘in’, ‘on’ or ‘under’. In the early years, learning about length is key to developing an understanding of proximity and provides a useful context for learning about fractions.

Teaching advice

Position

The language and associated vocabulary developed regarding position are important both within the topic of position itself, and for use with other mathematical concepts. Words and phrases such as ‘next to’, ‘before’ and ‘after’ can be used both in a physical world context and also in more abstract contexts. For example, in position – the chair is next to the table or the teacher entered the room before the students, whereas in number – 13 comes before 14, or 20 is next to 19 on the chart.

Positional language should be addressed regularly to enable students to develop a deep understanding of when and how to use these words. A variety of physical, digital and visual representations are helpful for some phrases such as ‘on top of’. On top of can be difficult as students may be confused between whether it means superimposed or above (see images below).

There are two main ideas associated with position for students in Early Stage 1:

  • following an instruction to position an object or themselves
  • describing the relative position of an object or themselves.

Some students may be able to describe the position of an object in relation to themselves, but not in relation to another object. The concept of position has strong vocabulary demands that are detailed below.

Ordinals

Ordinal number words such as ‘first’, ‘second’ and ‘third' represent a position in a sequence. They are different from whole numbers, which represent quantity. Ordinal numbers are introduced in relevant contexts, such as games, storytelling or recording the date.

Left and right

In Early Stage 1, students learn to use the terms ‘left’ and ‘right’ to describe position in relation to themselves. Teachers can assist students’ understanding of left and right by referencing a dominant hand or foot. The terms ‘left’ and ‘right’ depend on the frame of reference (which way an individual is facing) and can be a source of confusion for several years.

Typically, students are not expected to use ‘left’ or ‘right’ to describe the position of an object from the perspective of a person facing in the opposite direction until Stage 1. However, students who have mastered the concept of left and right in relation to themselves might be introduced to this idea.

Some students with perceptual difficulties and poor spatial awareness may experience difficulties with the concept of position. Modelling, and the use of visual cues, can support these students to follow or describe position.

Conversely, some students have well-developed skills in applying the concept of position, even if they do not yet have the language to articulate it. For example, some Aboriginal students may demonstrate a high degree of spatial awareness on a larger scale, such as in the local area or on-Country. Students may be supported by explicit teaching of mathematical language associated with spatial positioning.

Length

Early Stage 1 students often develop an awareness of the attribute of length by comparing objects of different lengths. Early Stage 1 focuses on the importance of accurately aligning one end of each object being compared. Where possible, students need experience with physically aligning the ends of two objects to compare their lengths. Start with comparing objects where the difference in lengths is easy to notice, for example the table is longer than the pencil. 

When items are closer in length, aligning the ends becomes necessary. For example comparing the height of two students by standing them back-to-back or aligning the ends of the two pencils.

Conservation of length is an important concept. It develops over time when students are comparing lengths. If students consistently say that the objects are equal in length, though their relative positions have been altered, they are conserving length.

Introducing fractions through length

Many students find understanding fractions, and particularly fraction magnitudes, to be one of the most challenging concepts in mathematics. The concept of a fraction is based on the process of division, rather than counting parts. To assist students in developing the process of division and its relationship to fractions, the continuous linear model of fractions is addressed in the concept of length.

The syllabus introduces fractions through equal sharing, using continuous and discrete models. This lays the foundations for fractions as indicating division and fractions as numbers.

Half

Half can be interpreted as dividing one whole into two equal pieces (continuous) or dividing a collection into two equal groups (discrete). The process is applied in early models of halving lengths and discrete quantities.

See Forming groups for discrete models of fractions.

The idea of a halfway point builds on the equality of two lengths. It also introduces the notion of subdividing a length, which in turn underpins measuring. It is important to model and reinforce the language of two equal lengths when describing ‘halfway’ and to provide non-examples where the lengths are not equal.

Further advice is available in Introducing fractions: Sharing (linked with division).

Some students with poor visual perception and difficulties with fine motor skills may require additional support to manipulate items and compare lengths. Strategies that can support these students include:

  • using visual cues such as a sticker or object to indicate the start and end of lengths
  • outlining boundaries of an image in bold
  • selecting colours that give a good colour contrast between background and foreground if using images of lengths
  • participating in activities that require hand–eye coordination.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of length and half a length, could be extended in their learning by finding other fractions of lengths such as repeatedly halving to find quarters, or exploring folding to make thirds.

Language

Students may need practice with the language of length in a variety of contexts. Young students often use general terms such as ‘big’ when they mean ‘tall’. They may know the word ‘fat’, but not the word ‘thick’. The terms ‘big’ and ‘long’ are sometimes used for specific attributes such as:

  • height
  • width
  • depth
  • length
  • thickness.

Engage students in activities that develop clarity in expressing distinct mathematical concepts. Providing examples and non-examples, including through the use of the Frayer model, can support students’ understanding of these mathematical concepts. See Vocabulary and language in Mathematics K–6 (Word, 16 pages, 1.14MB) for a further explanation, examples and non-examples.

Teachers can support students to use the language of mathematics by developing understanding that the same word can be used in a range of contexts. Some students may use ‘big’ to signify importance or ‘biggest’ to indicate intensity, such as those who use Aboriginal English. Making connections between concepts, and ensuring that students know when the context is mathematical, can support students to select the most appropriate term to use.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • position
  • between/next to/behind
  • inside/outside
  • left/right
  • directions
  • length
  • end/end to end
  • side by side
  • long/longer than/longest
  • short/shorter than/shortest
  • high/higher than/highest
  • tall/taller than/tallest
  • low/lower than/lowest
  • the same as
  • near/nearer
  • far/further
  • close/closer
  • whole
  • equal parts
  • half/halves/about halfway
  • more than a half/less than a half.

system.name: MS ES1 Teaching advice for Geometric measure

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

The units of measurement in Mass (g, kg) and Time (min, sec) do not rely on a physical spatial structure. In Mass, the spatial arrangement of the units does not affect the total weight. This is different to area or length where the arrangement of the units matter – they need to be end to end with no gaps.

In Early Stage 1, it is important that students develop an awareness of the attribute of mass and some of the language used to describe mass.

Concepts of time and duration are influenced by students’ experiences, cultural knowledge and personal judgements. Time can be understood and represented in a range of ways such as lunar, seasonal and Gregorian calendar systems, or linear and cyclical concepts of time.

Teaching advice

While Mass and Time are organised under the same substrand, it is not intended that teachers make connections across concepts in each of Time and Mass.

Mass

Early experiences often lead students to the conclusion that:

  • large things are heavier than small things, and
  • if two things are the same size and shape, they will have the same mass.

However, mass is not a spatial measure. Objects with the same volume can have different masses.

Students in Early Stage 1 should only be asked to compare two objects that are quite different in mass. Students need experiences with objects that are:

  • light and large
  • heavy and large
  • light and small
  • heavy and small
  • large but lighter than a smaller object.

Recognising that students may have different gross motor skills, teachers may need to provide a variety of experiences in order to support students to experience mass. These experiences could include:

  • feeling resistance against the body to determine if something is heavy or light
  • using grip to identify the mass of an object, using the terms ‘lighter’ or ‘heavier’
  • placing an object, such as a blanket, on the student’s lap to determine if the object is light or heavy.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of mass could be extended in their learning by exploring the placement of mass at different points on an equal-arm balance.

Time

Duration

An understanding of duration is introduced through ideas such as:

  • before
  • after
  • how long
  • how soon.

In Early Stage 1 time spans are personal judgements. Moments in time include ideas such as:

  • daytime
  • today
  • days of the week.

Students can be supported to develop an understanding of time by introducing time in everyday contexts, for example:

  • wait times for activities
  • duration of preferred activities, eg using timers
  • schedule of familiar routines, eg first-and-then board, visual schedule
  • identifying days of the week through regular weekly routines, eg sports, music
  • identifying activities done before and after school, eg night-time routines.

Telling time

In Early Stage 1, telling time focuses on reading hour time on analog and digital clocks. It draws on:

  • numeral recognition
  • position
  • spatial comparison.

Analog and digital clocks can be shown either through real objects or visual representations. When engaging with analog or digital clocks, it is important to ensure these displays are accessible. Consider using:

  • strong colour contrast between the hour and minute hands to improve visibility
  • braille, tactile or talking clocks.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of time could be extended in their learning by representing times on analog and digital clocks.

Schools are encouraged to work in partnership with their local Aboriginal community(ies) to develop understanding about Aboriginal concepts of time and associated language and terminology. This can assist teachers to support students in developing their understanding of content related to time.

Language

The terms ‘weigh’ and ‘weight’ are more common in everyday usage than ‘mass’. When working with students in Early Stage 1 ‘weight’ is an acceptable description for mass. Weight is a force that changes with gravity, while mass remains constant.

Hefting is testing the weight of an object by lifting or holding and balancing it. Where possible, students can use their bodies to balance two objects and compare the weight of each, for example holding one object in each hand.

The words ‘long’ and ‘short’ can be confusing to students who have only experienced these words in terms of length measurement. Students need experience with these words in both the context of length and time. Teachers should be mindful that the terms ‘long’ and ‘short’ are comparatives. Students might consider 5 years, 5 000 years, or 50 000 years to be a long time.

Some students, including Aboriginal students, may distinguish historical from contemporary time scales. For example, students may use additional qualifiers or alternative terms, such as ‘very long’, ‘long, long time ago’ or ‘old time’.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • mass
  • matter
  • heavy/heavier/heaviest
  • light/lighter/lightest
  • about the same as
  • hard to push/hard to pull
  • daytime/night-time
  • yesterday/today/tomorrow
  • before/after/next
  • a long time/a short time
  • days/week
  • weekdays/weekend days
  • time
  • morning/afternoon
  • clock
  • analog/digital
  • hands (of a clock)
  • o'clock.

system.name: MS ES1 Teaching advice for Non-spatial measure

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Concepts related to three-dimensional space are important to functioning in the world. Three-dimensional spatial structure is foundational for developing skills and processes related to position and location, perspective, and directions.

The manipulation of a variety of 3D objects supports the development of visual imagery, language and representation. Manipulation of 3D objects and observing them from different viewpoints leads to the development of skills in identifying the structural features of objects.

Students learn to understand volume as related to the measurement of three-dimensional space, in the same way that area relates to the measurement of two-dimensional space. Students need to explore the concept of volume as part of identifying and quantifying attributes of an object. Learning to compare internal volumes of containers and volumes of objects (how much space they take up) develops important estimation skills.

Teaching advice

3D geometric objects

In Early Stage 1, the emphasis is on students manipulating, describing, sorting and representing familiar geometric objects. Teachers are encouraged to use a range of objects of different sizes. Some students may require larger objects to manipulate.

Students should also be encouraged to describe the features of familiar objects using the terms ‘flat’, ‘round’ or ‘curved’. This prepares students to sort objects based on particular attributes, such as size, shape or function.

In developing students’ skills in reasoning about spatial relations, students should engage in tasks where they predict the stacking capabilities of various objects.

Volume and internal volume (capacity)

The attribute of volume is the amount of space occupied by an object or substance. The internal volume or capacity is only used in relation to containers and generally refers to liquid measurement. Knowing these definitions is not an expectation at this stage in learning.

In Early Stage 1, comparisons are made directly, using methods such as pouring or packing the contents of one container into another. Students can engage in pouring and filling containers with water or sand.

Early experiences often lead students to the conclusion that taller containers hold more. To develop beyond this, students need to directly compare containers that are:

  • shorter and hold more
  • taller and hold less
  • shorter and hold less
  • taller and hold more
  • short and hold the same as a tall container.

Many opportunities to emphasise the concepts of volume and capacity occur throughout the school day.

Students may be involved in stacking objects:

  • packing up toys
  • making models
  • storing objects in cupboards.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of volume could be extended in their learning by exploring different ways of stacking 24 cubes (eg 3 by 2 by 4 or 6 by 2 by 2).

Language

Students often need meaningful practice in using the general word container to include objects such as bottles, jars and tubs.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • object
  • shape
  • size
  • curved/flat
  • pointy/round
  • roll/slide
  • stack
  • container
  • liquid
  • empty/full/about half full
  • volume
  • space
  • has more/has less
  • will hold more/will hold less
  • takes up more space.

images.description: Line drawing of a chevron shape.
Line drawing of a kite shape.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

The development of two-dimensional spatial structure includes an ability to identify, rotate, orient and visualise shapes. These spatial skills are foundational for developing mathematical understanding related to the array structure of multiplication and area, map interpretation, visualisation and geometric reasoning (Lowrie et al. 2021). 

Features and properties of shapes also contribute to understanding the connection between two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects and spaces.

Students entering Early Stage 1 typically bring an understanding of shapes, which includes both regular and irregular shapes. In Early Stage 1, students also develop an awareness of the attribute of area through covering activities. Students’ knowledge and skills in spatial reasoning develop as they engage with content related to shape and area.

Teaching advice

2D shape

Students should be given time to explore and represent shapes in a range of contexts, such as:

  • identifying shapes in the classroom, school and local environment
  • representing shapes through painting, drawing, movements, gestures, writing, cutting and pasting.

It is important to select or create images of shapes that give a good colour contrast between background and foreground. This will assist students to see the images clearly and support students with visual difficulties.

Features of shapes

Children first learn that the question, What shape is this? is answered by words such as ‘circle’ and ‘square’. They then associate these shape words with initial examples. The initial examples contribute to the prototype image students hold for a shape. The equilateral triangle is a common prototype image for a triangle. This has meant that some students identify a right-angled triangle as half a triangle (Hourigan and Leavy 2015). For this reason it is important for teachers to introduce all types of triangles.

To develop a robust concept of shapes it is important that students encounter shapes in different orientations and sizes, represented in a variety of ways. Templates from which students create shapes can help to reinforce their understanding of the features of shapes and support developing students’ skills in reasoning about spatial relations.

Non-examples

In addition to showing students examples of a shape, providing non-examples of the shape helps focus their attention on the critical attributes. The non-examples should be similar to the examples, but without the defining characteristic of the shapes.

For example, a triangle with the defining characteristic of the number of sides, could be compared to:

Shape NameShape
Chevron
Kite

Students who require additional support to identify shapes may first need to be introduced to non-examples with significantly different characteristics. Match-to-sample activities can also support the understanding of the features of particular shapes. Students can be presented with a correct sample and one or two non-examples to begin with, with the number of non-examples increasing as students’ understanding develops.

In Early Stage 1, students should work with asymmetric or irregular shapes as well as regular shapes. Students are not expected to use the terms ‘regular’ and ‘irregular’ themselves.

See Vocabulary and language in Mathematics K–6 (Word, 16 pages, 1.14MB) for a further explanation of teaching concepts using examples and non-examples.

Area

Students should be given opportunities to compare:

  • two similar shapes of different areas where one fits inside the boundary of the other
  • two different-shaped areas where one can be placed on top of the other
  • two different shapes with the same area where one shape can be cut up and pasted onto the other.

Students who have already demonstrated an understanding of area could be extended in their learning by:

  • comparing shapes with similar areas that cannot be superimposed on each other
  • predicting and finding two shapes that might have the same area
  • learning to measure area.

Language

The term ‘shape’ is used in the syllabus to refer to a two-dimensional figure. ‘Object’ is used to refer to a three-dimensional solid or geometric form.

There are two different strategies that students can use to compare area by placing one on top of another. These are: superimposing and superposing.

Superimpose: comparison of areas by placing one area on top of another. 

Superpose: comparison of areas by aligning the edges (or corners) of two areas when one is placed on top of the other. 

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • shape/closed shape
  • circle
  • triangle
  • square
  • rectangle
  • features
  • side
  • line/curve
  • area
  • surface
  • inside/outside
  • bigger than/smaller than/the same as.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

A chance event is something that happens without a clear cause. Randomness is a difficult concept to grasp, even for adults. We tend to see patterns in data, even where none exist. By the end of Stage 1 students should typically be able to acknowledge the existence of a range of possible outcomes for an event. They should also be able to express the idea that some events are more likely to occur than others.

Teaching advice

Encourage students to recognise the impact of chance on predictions they make.

Certainty

When considering certainty, there are two extremes:

  • events that are certain to happen
  • events that are certain not to happen.

Words such as 'might', 'may' and 'possible' describe events between these two extremes.

Students often need assistance to develop an understanding of the terms ‘certain’ or ‘impossible’. Some students interpret events with a low probability as being impossible.

The idea of impossible, particularly in social contexts, is a more difficult concept for students than more likely or equally likely. Although we might not expect a coin toss to result in a coin standing on its edge, it is not impossible. It is the aggregation of all of the possible outcomes that really means an event is certain or impossible.

Sample space

To address notions of chance, it is often best to use examples where all the things that can happen, sometimes called the sample space, are well defined. Students often do not realise that for something to be impossible there must be none present at all in the sample space, the set of all possible outcomes. Determining the sample space (that is, what is possible) is the essential first step in understanding any probability problem.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • possible
  • might happen
  • likely/unlikely/more likely.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

In society, there is a constant need to understand, interpret and analyse information displayed in tables or graphical forms. Students need to recognise how information may be displayed in a misleading way, resulting in drawing the wrong conclusions about the data. Experiences with collecting, organising, displaying, and analysing data assist students in developing graphical and statistical literacy skills (Watson and Callingham 2003).

Early experiences with data should be based on real-life contexts relevant to the students and connected to other curriculum areas such as History, Geography, or Science and Technology. Students should be encouraged to ask questions relevant to their experiences and interests and to design ways of investigating their questions. Students develop effective data collection and display methods to present data in a variety of ways.

Teaching advice

Representing an object with a different object, picture or drawing is an abstraction.

It is important that each object in a (one-to-one) data display represents one object. One object can also represent an idea, such as a person's preference.

Aligning the rows or columns of images to form a common baseline in a picture graph can make comparisons easier.

Collecting data

When collecting information to investigate a question, students can develop simple ways of recording. Some methods include:

  • placing blocks or counters in a line
  • colouring squares on grid paper
  • using tally marks.

Tally marks

A single mark in a tally represents 1 observation. Tally marks are usually drawn in groups of five. The first four marks are often drawn vertical, with the fifth mark drawn diagonally through the first four. This makes counting in groups more efficient. For example:

Tally marksRepresents
3
5
9

Different countries use different systems of tally marks. Cultures using Chinese characters tally five by making 正.

Data in categories

Categorical data means the information being collected can be separated into distinct groups or categories. Examples include:

  • the colours of Smarties in a box
  • class members’ favourite fruits.

Students may engage more effectively with collecting data through observation or conversation, rather than questioning. Some Aboriginal students, for a number of cultural and historical reasons, may prefer not to ask or be asked direct questions, or may have well-developed observational skills that could be applied through learning activities related to collecting data.

Some students may experience difficulty accessing visual representations of data. These students can be supported by presenting data in alternate formats and through the use of assistive technology, including screen readers.

When using visual texts such as images, picture graphs, lists and tables, it is important to ensure these are accessible. Consider using:

  • strong colour contrast to improve visibility
  • alternative text and captions to provide descriptions.

Some students may also experience difficulty with conceptually understanding visual representations of data. In these instances, visual information can be introduced to students using their preferred method of communication, for example:

  • real objects
  • photos of real objects
  • images of objects
  • abstract images or drawings.

This provides opportunities for students to develop their understanding of the language used in data displays and attribute meaning between the visual representation and the data.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • information
  • data
  • collect
  • gather
  • display
  • symbol
  • tally mark
  • picture graph.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Forming groups helps students progress from counting by ones to skip counting and using repeated addition. These are important steps towards the idea of coordinating units and understanding multiplication.

Teaching advice

Rhythmic and skip counting

Number words sequences for fives and tens produce a rhythm. This rhythm can be used in choral counting. Skip counting by two can develop from counting aloud and:

  • stressing each second number: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 …
  • skipping over the non-stressed numbers: 2, 4, 6 …

Division

There are two forms of division associated with forming groups:

DivisionTypeMeaningExample
Equal SharingPartitiveHow many in each group?If 12 marbles are shared between three students, how many does each student get?
Equal groupingQuotitiveHow many groups are there?If I have 12 marbles and each child is to get four, how many children will get marbles?

Understanding grouping division is important to make sense of dividing by a quantity less than one (eg 8 ÷ 0·5) which students encounter in Stage 4.

After students have divided a quantity into equal groups (eg twelve objects divided into groups of four) they should recombine the groups. This reversal of the process links multiplication and division.

When sharing a collection of objects into two groups, students may describe the number of objects in each group as being one half of the whole collection.

Arrays

An array is one of several different arrangements that can be used to model multiplicative situations involving whole numbers.

An array is made by arranging a set of objects, such as counters or pictures, into columns and rows:

  • each column must contain the same number of items as the other columns
  • each row must contain the same number of items as the other rows.

Students should focus on using groups of, before progressing to rows of and columns of. Although the array is a powerful mathematical model, it requires students to identify groups in two directions. Coordinating between columns and rows is much more difficult than using groups of with repeated addition.

Composite units

A composite unit is a unit-whole composed of other units. A unit of 10 things is a composite unit if it can be interpreted as both one 10 (a single unit) and 10 individual units at the same time. A model of a composite unit would be one pea pod containing 10 peas.

In developing an understanding of a group acting as composite it is helpful to distinguish between the number of groups and the number in each group as this can be confusing for students.

Introducing fractions: Equal sharing (linked with division)

Many students find understanding fractions, and in particular fraction magnitudes, one of the most challenging concepts in learning mathematics.

Fractions are introduced through equal-sharing problems. As Empson and Levi (2011) stated, ‘If models do not draw on children’s formative experiences of sharing and partitioning, then they are likely to prevent teachers from cultivating the natural insights about quantities that young children have’.

Students can later connect the words and symbols for fractions to the parts created in the process of solving the problems. The concept of a fraction is then based on the process of division, rather than counting parts. This lays the foundations for fractions as indicating division and fractions as numbers.

Equal sharing begins with sharing between two. The process of halving is applied in early models of halving lengths (see Geometric measure) and discrete quantities in forming groups. To assist students in seeing the link between the two models, linear arrangements of discrete quantities are used.

Some students may have prior knowledge and understanding of fractions and dividing objects equally among groups. For example, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students may have an understanding of the concept of fractions as it relates to kinship and community responsibilities.

Language

Check that students are familiar with groups of two like things being called pairs.

Avoid using the term ‘lots of’ when describing grouping for multiplication. It can be confusing to students because of its everyday use, for example ‘lots of fish in the sea'.

Formal writing of number sentences for multiplication and division, including the use of the symbols × and ÷ is not introduced until Stage 2.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to determine if a student can use the structure of equal groups to solve multiplication problems and group for division (this activity was also described in Early Stage 1 Forming groups).

[Provide students with a pile of at least 20 unifix cubes]

Can you make 5 towers, with 3 blocks in each tower?

How many towers do you have?

How many blocks in each tower?

How many altogether?

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • group
  • number of groups/number in each group
  • row/column
  • number of rows/number of columns
  • number in each row/number in each column
  • array
  • sharing/shared between
  • left over
  • total
  • equal
  • half/quarter/eighth
  • one-half/one-quarter/one-eighth
  • halve.

Why is it important?

Forming groups helps students progress from counting by ones to skip counting and using repeated addition. These are important steps towards the idea of coordinating units and understanding multiplication.

Rhythmic and skip counting

title.value: Teaching advice for Forming groups B

system.name: MS S1 Teaching advice for Forming groups B

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Being able to describe the relative positions of objects in a picture or diagram requires interpretation of a two-dimensional representation. In Stage 1, measuring the lengths of objects using uniform informal units enables students to develop some key understandings of measurement.

Teaching advice

Position

In Early Stage 1, students used the terms ‘left’ and ‘right’ to describe position in relation to themselves. In Stage 1, many students begin to use the terms ‘left’ and ‘right’ to describe position from the perspective of a person facing in the opposite direction.

Length

Understandings involved in measuring the lengths of objects include:

  • units should be repeatedly placed end to end without gaps or overlaps
  • units must be equal in size
  • identical units should be used to compare lengths
  • some units are more appropriate for measuring particular objects
  • there is a relationship between the size of the chosen unit and the number of units needed.

Make, mark and move

Using the phrase make, mark and move assists students in understanding the concept of repeated units. By placing a unit on a flat surface, marking where it ends, moving it along and continuing the process, students identify that the unit of measurement is the space between the marks on a measuring device and not the marks themselves.

Conserving length

Recognising that a length may be divided and recombined to form the same length is an important component of conserving length.

Estimating length

Estimating length is often based on visualising a known unit or benchmark. The units might be personal measures such as finger-widths or handspans.

Before students are asked to estimate lengths and distances it is important that students:

  • have had some measurement experiences
  • are taught a variety of estimation strategies.

To estimate longer distances, teachers may ask students to imagine how many times a metre ruler could be laid end to end across the space. To assist with this method of estimating, have one student measure out the distance being estimated with a metre ruler. Allow students to adjust their estimates after the first metre is measured and again at about halfway.

Students may have prior knowledge or experience with measurement and estimating length. For example, some Aboriginal students may have a sense of measurement based on their cultural knowledge or on-Country experiences. Teachers are encouraged to further develop their knowledge, and engage in meaningful exchange with students to support making connections with Western concepts of measurement.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • length
  • distance
  • end/end to end
  • side by side
  • gap
  • overlap
  • measure
  • estimate
  • unit
  • handspan.

Suggestions for determining key progress points

The following activity can be used to determine if a student can identify the halfway point of a journey. This question relates to both length and fractions and builds on the content in Early Stage 1.

An ant crawls around the outside of this triangle [teacher gestures around the sides of the triangle]:

If each side of the triangle is the same length, can you show where the ant will be when it is half of the way around the triangle from the start?

Starting from the base emphasises the need to find half of the distance around the triangle rather than halving the triangle.

title.name: 📜 Title
title.value: Teaching advice for Geometric measure A

system.name: MS S1 Teaching advice for Geometric measure A

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Length

Formal units of length

Students should be given opportunities to apply their understanding of measurement, gained through experiences with the use of uniform informal units, to experiences with the use of the centimetre and metre.

They could make a measuring device using uniform informal units before using a ruler, eg using a length of 10 connecting cubes. This would assist students in understanding that the distances between marks on a ruler represent unit lengths and that the marks indicate the endpoints of each unit. Half of a length of 10 connecting cubes provides a link to simple fractions.

Fractional lengths

In Stage 1, fractions are formed by the process of division rather than counting parts. Fractional parts, halves, quarters and eighths are formed in two different ways:

  • equal parts of a whole length
  • equal quantities of a linear arrangement of a collection of objects.

In focusing on repeated halving, emphasise that the size of the resulting fractional part will depend on the size of the original whole length or collection of objects. It is not necessary for students in Stage 1 to use the symbol ½ to mean one-half or use ¼ for one-quarter.

Three models of fractions

Continuous model (linear)

The continuous model (linear) should be introduced first. It uses one-directional cuts or folds that compare fractional parts based on length. It is helpful to highlight the long edge to focus on length.

Continuous model (area)

This model uses multi-directional cuts or folds to compare fractional parts to the whole. This model should be introduced once students understand the concept of area developed in Stage 2. Folding to show equivalent area relies on a shape having an axis of symmetry for the fold line.

Discrete model

This model uses separate items in collections to represent parts of the whole group.

Language

When recording measurements, a space should be left between the number and the abbreviated unit, eg 3 cm, not 3cm.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • metre
  • centimetre.

title.value: Teaching advice for Geometric measure B

system.name: MS S1 Teaching advice for Geometric measure B

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Measuring mass using informal units enables students to develop some key understandings of measurement. These include:

  • needing to repeatedly use a unit as a measuring device
  • selecting an appropriate unit for a specific task
  • appreciating that a common informal unit is necessary for comparing the masses of objects
  • understanding that some informal units (eg pebbles) are unsatisfactory because they are not uniform.

To have a better understanding of duration, it is important in Stage 1 that students develop a sense of:

  • one hour
  • one minute
  • one second.

Sense of time is developed through practical experiences, rather than simply recalling that there are 60 minutes in an hour.

Teaching advice

Mass

Mass is an intrinsic property of an object, but its most common measure is in terms of weight. Weight is a force that changes with gravity, while mass remains constant.

When students realise that changing the shape of an object does not alter its mass, they are said to conserve the property of mass.

Hefting and balancing

Hefting is testing the weight of an object by lifting and balancing it. Where possible, students can compare the weights of two objects by using their bodies to balance each object, eg holding one object in each hand. 

The equal-arm balance can have two functions:

  • comparing the masses of two objects
  • measuring the mass of an object by using multiple identical units.

Recognising that students may have different gross motor skills, a variety of experiences may need to be provided in order to support students to experience the concepts of hefting and balancing. This could include comparing the masses of two objects using grip or resistance. Students should be provided with sufficient time to process the instruction and manipulate their body appropriately in order to feel the mass of an object.

Time

In Stage 1, telling time focuses on reading the half-hour and quarter of an hour on both analog and digital clocks. While digital clocks are more common than analog clocks, the latter are more effective in representing the 60-minute base of 1 hour.

The representation of a half-hour as 30 minutes or halfway around the clockface is more transparent to the underlying base than a digital representation. The digital representation 7:30 relies on recognising that :30 means half an hour (rather than :50, for example).

The representation of a quarter past the hour as 15 minutes or one quarter around the clockface and quarter to the hour as 45 minutes or three-quarters around the clockface is a much more challenging concept than half-hour for many students. It will require extensive modelling and repeated practice.

Students need to be aware that there is always more than one way of expressing a particular time, for example:


Analog clocks can also be connected with concepts of time cycles, such as weekly, monthly, annual, seasonal or lunar cycles.

Language

As the terms ‘weigh’ and ‘weight’ are common in everyday usage, they can be accepted in student language should they arise.

An equal-arm balance consists of a pivoted horizontal lever of equal length arms, called the beam, with a weighing pan suspended from each arm.

The terms ‘hour hand’ and ‘minute hand’, rather than ‘little hand’ and ‘big hand’, should be used to promote understanding of their respective functions.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • measure
  • estimate
  • is the same as/about the same as
  • level balance/equal-arm balance
  • mass
  • heavy/heavier
  • light/lighter
  • balance
  • calendar
  • days
  • date
  • month/year
  • time
  • clock
  • analog/digital
  • hour hand/minute hand
  • o'clock
  • half past
  • hour
  • minute
  • second
  • quarter past/quarter to
  • numeral.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Volume

When students build rectangular prisms from cubes, they have a context for using the language of 3D objects such as edge or face. Drawing can also help link practical activities such as stacking cubes to diagrams and plans.

Volume concepts are more difficult to visualise than length or area as some units will be hidden by the layer structure.

Constructing and/or drawing different prisms that can be made from a fixed number of cubes, such as 24, gives students opportunities to become familiar with the layer structure of volume and to represent the structure as they interpret it.

Working out the volume based on the number of blocks in a row or column of blocks and the number of rows in a layer depends on systematic packing.

Knowledge of the structure of rows and columns in two dimensions, learnt as part of the area concept, will assist students to learn about the structure of three-dimensional packing.

Language

3D objects

In 3D geometry, the term ‘edge’ refers to the interval formed where two faces of a three-dimensional object meet.

The term ‘vertex’ (plural: ‘vertices’) can refer to the point where three or more faces of a three-dimensional object meet or where two straight sides of a two-dimensional shape meet.

These concepts can be taught using examples and non-examples. See Vocabulary and language in Mathematics K–6 (Word, 16 pages, 1.14MB).

title.name: 📜 Title
title.value: Teaching advice for Three-dimensional spatial structure B

system.name: MS S1 Teaching advice for Three-dimensional spatial structure B

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
2D shape

In Stage 1, students need to have experiences involving directions and turning. Explain and discuss what represents:

  • a full-turn
  • a half-turn
  • a quarter-turn.

Relating this information to students physically may be helpful. For example, play games such as 'Simon Says' with Simon saying to make turns. Students may benefit from linking the vocabulary of half-turns and quarter-turns to their experiences with clocks.

Digital technologies such as computer drawing tools may use terms like ‘rotate’ and ‘flip horizontal’ to describe transformations. The icons for these functions may assist students in locating the required transformations.

Area

In covering activities, rectangular shapes are used so that students develop an understanding of the structure of the unit covering (array) in area. Knowledge of array structure is important for an understanding of area measurement. It enables the area of a rectangle to be linked to the lengths of its sides. Consequently, it provides the basis for rectangular area to be calculated using multiplication.

To assist students to develop an appreciation of the structure of repeated units in measuring area, teaching progresses from providing multiple squares to cover an area to providing only one square. Having only one square requires students to create the pattern or structure of the units by drawing or visualising.

Drawing the array structure for the tessellation of area units appears to assist students to perceive the rows (and columns) as composite units. This perception enables them to connect side length and area. If students have drawn and talked about the structure of an array, then the structure of three-dimensional stacking may be grasped more easily.

Language

2D shape

In Stage 1, students are introduced to the terms:

  • slide (or translation)
  • reflection
  • rotation.

In Stage 2, students are expected to use the term ‘translate’ more consistently. It is important students realise that these transformations do not change the area of the shapes.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate:

  • turn
  • full-turn
  • half-turn
  • quarter-turn
  • left turn
  • right turn
  • clockwise
  • anti-clockwise.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
The equals sign

The equals sign identifies a relationship in mathematics.

Students need to be provided with contexts to appreciate that the = sign is a statement of equality. For example, 4 + 1 = 3 + 2 means 4 + 1 'has the same value as' 3 + 2.

Gesturing when teaching can help students appreciate the 2 sides in an equality relationship.

For example:

‘I want to make one side, [sweeping left hand back and forth under the left side of the equality], equal to the other side, [sweeping right hand back and forth under the right side of the equality].’

Gesturing in this way can encourage students to produce similar gestures, which can aid learning.

A sequence of True or False equality statements can be used to encourage discussion in class.

For example, show each of the following statements one at a time and ask if this is true or false, and how do you know?

4 + 7 = 11

11 = 4 + 7

11 = 11

4 + 7 = 4 + 7

4 + 7 = 7 + 4

4 + 7 = 5 + 6

Emphasise that  ‘=’ means ‘has the same value as’.

Using an analogy of a balance can help some students broaden their understanding of equality.

Typically, students initially interpret the equals sign as an operational symbol meaning the answer or the total. This meaning has been found to change gradually to include interpreting it as a relational symbol of equivalence in certain contexts (McNeil and Alibali 2005).

Connecting addition and subtraction

If you add 2 numbers, the total is the sum of the parts. The additive relationship can be expressed as an equality, such as 45 + 23 = 68 or 68 = 45 + 23. This equality also highlights how addition is related to subtraction.

Knowing 45 and 23 add to 68 also means the difference between 68 and 45 is 23. The connection between addition and subtraction means that addition can be used to carry out subtraction.

To work out 68 − 45, think: How much must be added to 45 to make 68?

The principle of equality also means numbers can be partitioned in different ways, which can make some addition questions easier.

eg 500 + 670 is 670 = 500 + 170, so 500 + 670 = 500 + 500 + 170, which is 1000 + 170 = 1170.

The mental strategies students learn for addition and subtraction form the foundation for generalisable methods. Developing calculation methods that can be used with any numbers is an important component of number and algebra.

Developing a repertoire of strategies

In Stage 1, mental strategies progress from count-by-one methods, through counting-on, to using number bonds and bridging across multiples of ten. In Stage 2, students apply and extend their repertoire of mental strategies for addition and subtraction. The mental strategies are shared using models such as the bar model.

Different ways of representing models

Using number lines as a representation of additive relations is continued from Stage 1. Bar models and tape diagrams are also introduced in Stage 2 to assist students in appreciating and recognising the part-part-whole relationships when adding and subtracting. Representing the problems using bar diagrams can help reduce the load on working memory. Some students might need access to other forms of manipulatives to communicate or represent their learning.

Bar models and tape diagrams are very similar. A tape diagram looks like a single piece of tape and is used to show how quantities are related (Xiaobo and Harrington 2022).

Bar models can use separated rectangles rather than a single piece of tape.

Two additive uses of the bar model

One of the advantages of using a bar model to consistently represent the information in a problem is that students know what kind of picture to create to show what is known, and it ‘shows the student how to use that information to solve the problem’ (Hoven & Garelick 2007:28).

The bar model forms a foundation for algebra in helping students to represent problems symbolically.

The complement principle of additive relations

Additive reasoning is based on quantities being connected to form the whole.

This additive connection generates 2 basic principles: commutativity and the complement principle.

Commutativity refers to the order of addition not changing the result, 3 + 4 = 4 + 3.

The complement principle highlights the inverse relation between addition and subtraction.

That is, 3 + 4 = 7 implies 7 − 4 = 3 using the complement principle, or equally 7 − 3 = 4. An appreciation of commutativity appears to develop before making use of the complement principle (Ching and Nunes 2017).

The order in which these principles develop is likely influenced by students learning to count on from the larger number before learning to solve ‘missing addend’, or missing value, questions.

In symbols, 4 + □ = 10 is a missing addend question.

The strategy of counting on from the larger number relies on the commutative principle of addition, whereas the complement principle is used in solving ‘missing addend’ questions.

Using the complement principle with subtraction

The most challenging use of the complement principle is recognising that a – b = c means a – c = b. The number of steps of algebraic reasoning needed to appreciate why the two forms are equivalent makes substantial demands on working memory.

For example, 100 – 3 = 97 implies 100 – 97 = 3 because 97 + 3 = 100.

Image long description: A diagram representing the complement principle used with subtraction. It shows the relation of the quantities 97 and 100.

This use of the complement principle requires recognising that when 2 numbers are added, subtracting either number from the total produces its complement, that is, the number required to make a group complete.

title.name: 📜 Title
title.value: Teaching advice for Additive relations A

system.name: MS S2 Teaching advice for Additive relations A

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Understanding equality

Finding the missing number in a number sentence involving operations on both sides of the equals sign relies on understanding equality and the meaning of the equals sign (Falkner et al. 1999).

In solving 8 + 4 = □ + 5 the answers of 12, 17 or even 12 and 17, are often more commonly provided than the correct answer.

Understanding that equality means 2 mathematical expressions hold the same value is essential to symbolic algebra. However, this relational meaning of the equals sign typically develops over a number of years.

Developing an understanding of the equals sign through discussion of True and False number sentences should be revisited.

Which of the following number sentences are True (and how do you know)?




4 + 5 = 912 − 5 = 97 = 3 + 4
8 + 2 = 10 + 47 + 4 = 15 − 48 = 8

Early algebraic reasoning

Finding an unknown number in a number sentence is a form of early algebraic reasoning.

Early algebraic reasoning is characterised by calculating only with known numbers to find unknown quantities. More mature algebraic reasoning, such as in Stage 4, involves calculating using the unknown quantities (Filloy and Rojano 1989).

Why teach multidigit addition and subtraction?

The main point of teaching how to add or subtract multidigit numbers is not to provide students with a procedure to do calculations, but to provide students with an opportunity to deepen their understanding of our base-10 numeration system.

Regrouping

Before learning to record subtraction with regrouping, students start with addition that requires trading to form a higher value unit eg 10 ones is traded for 1 ten or 10 tens for 100.

In Stage 1, recordings made use of multiples of 10 as intermediate values when adding.

In Stage 2, recordings typically focus on groups of 10.

Developing an understanding of multidigit subtraction is generally more challenging than addition (Fuson and Burghardt 2003).

This is due to the lack of understanding of commutativity ie 7 − 2 is not the same as 2 − 7.

There are many ways to effectively develop conceptual understanding of multidigit addition and subtraction (Fuson et al. 1997).

For example, one approach focuses on counting by tens, using the arithmetic rack (rekenrek) or bead strings instead of using base-10 blocks.

Another approach uses Montessori number cards or place value arrow cards.

As well as learning how to add and subtract multidigit numbers, it is important that students can make informed choices on the use of computational procedures.

Research indicates that after one year of practising standard algorithms, students often apply the algorithms to questions which are better done using mental computation eg 527 + 399, 601 – 127 (Torbeyns and Verschaffel 2013).

Commonly used subtraction algorithms rely on regrouping. The algorithm can be explained using manipulatives, in which 10 is exchanged for 10 ones and 100 is exchanged for 10 tens, when regrouping is necessary.

However, various studies have shown that the use of concrete materials produces mixed results when it comes to conceptual understanding (Carbonneau et al. 2013).

How well the materials match the student’s concept of place value plays an important role in the effectiveness of materials like base-10 blocks.

If a student hasn’t yet developed a concept of 10 as a composite unit (both 10 ones and 1 ten), using base-10 blocks to represent regrouping will have little meaning.

Three categories of mental computation strategies for multidigit subtraction with regrouping

Strategy flexibility is identifying which strategies may fit with the numerical characteristics and demands of the different problem types.

Although there are different ways of describing mental computation strategies used with multidigit subtraction, the following 3 broad categories capture the common approaches (Hartnett 2007).

  • Sequential – left to right, for example:
    • 456 – 298 is 456 − 200 = 256, 256 − 90 = 166, 166 − 8 = 158
  • Decomposition – using indirect addition or building up, for example:
    • 456 – 298 is 8 + 8 = 16, 90 + 50 = 140, 300 + 100 = 400; 8 + 50 + 100 = 158
    • 456 – 298 is 458 − 300 = 158 (recognising 298 is 2 less than 300).

The same example has been used to demonstrate the differences between the methods.

This comparison of the different approaches highlights that the third method, using the constant difference to vary the question, can be most effective when the number being subtracted ends in an 8 or 9. Subtraction using indirect addition can be effective when the difference between the 2 numbers is small (eg 713 − 695).

From mental strategies to written algorithms

The ability to add two 2-digit numbers mentally by an efficient method is considered a crucial test of readiness for written computation (Ewbank 1977).

Mental calculation can help students understand how numbers ‘work’ and what their structure is, as well as aiding the understanding and development of written methods of calculation (Heirdsfield and Cooper 2004).

What is an algorithm?

An algorithm is a set of predefined steps used for a class of problems. The best-known algorithms are those associated with the 4 operations in arithmetic.

The most popular subtraction algorithm involving ‘trading units’ is known as the decomposition method* (Brownell and Moser 1949). It relies on partitioning and regrouping. To subtract 39 from 264 using column subtraction, the 264 is thought of as being decomposed into 2 hundreds, 6 tens and 4 ones. Then 1 ten is traded for 10 ones so that 264 is represented as 2 hundreds, 5 tens and 14 ones.

An advantage of expressing the numbers in an expanded form is that the exchange of units shows the size of the units. In contracted form, the size of the units is masked as it depends upon interpreting the positional value of the units and every trade appears as exchanging a ‘ten’.

Another algorithm for column subtraction is based on the principle that adding the same number to the number being subtracted ie the subtrahend and the minuend, does not alter the difference.1

This method for column subtraction with trading is known as equal additions and involves adding ten to both numbers.

For example, 10 ones can be added to the minuend and 1 ten to the subtrahend without changing the difference between the 2.

Image long description: Column subtraction of 264 – 39, showing decomposition of 264 into its separate place values and using trading units.

The equal additions method relies on the principle of maintaining a constant difference.

Although there are other subtraction algorithms (eg the complement algorithm) the above 2 have been the most taught (Ellerton and Clements 2012).

Students have an opportunity to deepen their understanding of our base-10 numeration system through using expanded forms of the numbers involved.

* Compensation is a popular method of teaching subtraction because students find it easier to understand than other methods.

Limitations of vertical algorithms

Addition and subtraction problems involving single-digit numbers should not be written vertically. Writing a subtraction of a single-digit number from a 2-digit number in vertical form is not helpful.

Encouraging students to only use a vertical algorithm to operate with numbers can inhibit their development of number sense. Students who only use a vertical algorithm, may be less willing to attempt problems in alternative ways and can become afraid to take risks (Narode et al. 1993).

Misconceptions with vertical algorithms

One of the most common misconceptions associated with the subtraction algorithm is known as the smaller-from-larger error (Resnick 2020).

When students focus only on the values of the digits in the subtraction, some ‘simplify’ by reordering the terms to always subtract the smaller value from the larger digit.

Image long description: Column subtraction of 543  – 289 = 346, with arrows demonstrating the error of switching values when subtracting that requires trading, when students think they 'can't do' 3 - 9 so switch the digits.

Rather than regrouping 40 in 543 as 30 + 10, the response aligns with thinking, ‘I cannot take 9 from 3, so I’ll just take 3 from 9.’

Emphasising the quantity value of the digits and using number expanders can assist in addressing this error. Starting by estimating the answer can also help: Will the answer to the above subtraction be more than 300 or less than 300? Why?

Another common challenge with learning to use the vertical subtraction algorithm is dealing with zeros. Sometimes students believe that 0 means ‘nothing’, so it can be ignored.

A sequence for exchanging in subtraction

1. A 3-digit number minus a 2-digit number (exchanging tens for ones)

2. A 3-digit number minus a 2-digit number (exchanging hundreds for tens)

3. A 3-digit number minus a 2-digit number (exchanging tens for ones and hundreds for tens)

Image long description: Column subtraction of 311 – 27. Numbers are decomposed into place value, with tens exchanged for ones, and hundreds exchanged for tens.

4. A 3-digit number minus a 3-digit number (exchanging tens for ones)

5. A 3-digit number minus a 3-digit number (exchanging hundreds for tens)

6. A 3-digit number minus a 3-digit number (exchanging tens for ones and hundreds for tens)

Image long description: Column subtraction of 732 – 346. Numbers are decomposed into place value, with tens exchanged for ones, and hundreds exchanged for tens.

7. A 3-digit number minus a 3-digit number with a zero in the answer

8. A 3-digit number minus a 3-digit number with one zero in the top line

or 

Subtraction from a multiple of one hundred in the top line (such as 300 − 197) has not been included in this sequence as it is often easier to complete these subtractions mentally than with an algorithm.

Mental methods and vertical algorithms

Mental computation still needs to be emphasised even when students can use a formal written method. It is helpful to discuss which questions are better done mentally than using a vertical algorithm. For example, a question such as 2002 − 3 or 1000 − 999 is better done mentally than using a vertical algorithm.

Encourage students to consider the values of the numbers involved in an arithmetical operation before selecting a method to solve the problem (Lucenta and Kelemanik 2022).

Questions such as finding 20 − 19 + 18 − 17 + 16 − 15 + 14 − 13 + 12 − 11, can motivate students to reflect on the numbers involved in a question before calculating.

When developing a formal vertical algorithm, sequence the examples to cover the range of possibilities. The sequence should include questions without trading, questions with trading in one or more places, and questions with one or more zeros in the first number (particularly with subtraction).

For subtraction questions with one or more zeros in the first number, discuss whether the algorithm or mental computation is easier.

Random generators include coins, dice and spinners. The initial focus in Stage 2 is on random generators producing equally likely outcomes. For example, spinners with unequal areas do not have equally likely outcomes and are not addressed in Stage 2 Chance.

The process of identifying all possible outcomes, followed by predicting and testing, can help students to form a sense of the nature of chance. 

An important emerging understanding is that identifying the possible outcomes can help establish expectations, but the randomness in the experiment means that something different may happen.

Language

The everyday language of chance can be at odds with the precision required in mathematical language. Terms like ‘certain’ or ‘likely’ are used to indicate a possibility in speech, rather than having an exact probability value.

A chance ‘event’ might be selecting a coloured ball without looking, and the ‘outcome’ would be the colour of the ball (Figure 2).

In Figure 2, selecting a red, a blue or a yellow ball without looking are ‘equally likely’ outcomes. Note that ‘equally likely’ need not mean a 50–50 chance. For the above example, the balls need to be identical in all aspects except colour.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate: 

  • chance
  • experiment
  • outcome
  • random
  • trials
  • tally
  • expected results
  • actual results.

system.name: MS S2 Teaching advice for Chance A

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Expectation and variation

Randomness can lead to unexpected outcomes. The ‘law of averages’ is a term sometimes used to describe the common mistaken belief that an outcome must occur as many times as its numerical probability suggests. This belief suggests that what has happened in the past will be balanced by what occurs next. An example of the ‘law of averages’ is the belief that if a coin has come down heads 6 times in a row, it is likely to be tails on the next toss.

Theoretically, when a fair coin is tossed, there is an equal chance of obtaining a head or a tail. If the coin is tossed and 5 heads in a row are obtained, there is still an equal chance of a head or a tail on the next toss, since each toss is an independent event. It is not possible that the coin toss can be influenced by what has just happened, as it doesn’t know.

Students need many opportunities to compare their expectations (what might happen) with actual outcomes (what does happen) to appreciate the variation that is experienced with random generators.

Comparing likelihood

Comparing the likelihood of events depends upon a sense of proportion. Realising there is a greater likelihood of obtaining a ‘tail’ when tossing a coin than rolling a ‘6’ using standard dice, is based on intuitively comparing ratios. Comparing the likelihood of events should focus only on ratios that are very familiar to students.

Language

As described in Part A, everyday use of chance language is imprecise. It is not intended that precise measures of chance are assigned to commonly used terms such as ‘likely’ or ‘unlikely’. It is best to avoid activities of assigning precise positions on a number line to imprecise chance terms, such as ‘possible’.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate: 

  • chance
  • event
  • possible
  • impossible
  • likely
  • unlikely
  • less likely
  • more likely
  • most likely
  • least likely
  • equally likely
  • more often
  • less frequent
  • experiment
  • outcome.

Data can be acquired from the internet, newspapers or magazines, as well as through students' observations, surveys, votes and questionnaires.

The following information on types of data variables provides background knowledge for teaching. Stage 2 students are not expected to classify the type of data they are collecting.

Types of data

The characteristics or attributes that are observed, measured and recorded such as eye colour or height are called variables. In Stage 2, students work with discrete data which is either categorical or numerical.

Categorical data can be separated into distinct groups, eg colour, gender, blood type.

Discrete numerical data describes items or events that can be counted in whole number values, where values in between the whole numbers cannot be found or labelled in the data display. For example, the number of students in each class is an exact whole number amount. The value of a discrete variable is found by counting. In Stage 2, students focus on collecting and graphing discrete data.

Numerical data has variations that are expressed as numbers, eg the heights of students in a class, the number of children in families. Measuring height produces continuous numerical data while number of children in families is an example of discrete numerical data.

Organising and displaying data

Data can be displayed in tables and graphs. Students should be provided with opportunities to consider the use of tables and graphs in real-world contexts. Graphs are frequently used to persuade or influence the reader. A simple table showing counts is often the best way to display categorical data.

Column graphs consist of vertical columns or horizontal bars (Figure 1).

Column graphs are used to represent categorical and more generally, discrete numerical data. When creating column graphs, the columns should not be joined as they represent distinct categorical data.

The term 'bar graph' is reserved for divided bar graphs (Figure 2) and should not be used for a column graph with horizontal bars.

Dot plots

Dot plots are an alternative to a column graph when there are only a small number of data values. Each value is recorded as a dot so that the frequencies for each of the values can be counted easily.

Educational graphing software can provide a virtual environment to explore dot plots, enabling students to interact with and manipulate the data. Dot stickers are also useful resources for making colourful dot plots.

Continuous numerical data that changes over time is introduced in Stage 3, where students are provided with opportunities to collect and interpret continuous data. Line graphs are left to Stage 3 after students have learnt to use scales of many-to-one correspondence. Interpreting continuous data representations can involve estimating between scale values (eg values between two times of the day).

Language

The language of statistical reasoning

Statistical reasoning means understanding and being able to explain statistical processes and being able to interpret statistical results (Garfield 2002). It is the way people reason with statistical ideas and make sense of statistical information. Statistical reasoning may involve connecting one concept to another or combining ideas about data and chance (Watson 2004).

Inference is an important component of statistical reasoning. Learning what can be inferred from the data mirrors learning inference in reading. Inference in reading uses the information in the story to predict, while considering referential and logical relationships. When drawing on the activity of prediction from cues in storybooks, students might be asked to infer things such as a character’s feelings about failing to achieve their goal in a particular story episode, or to predict possible things the character might try to do next.

Encourage students to work through questions that start with what is in the data (‘here’) and move to what can be inferred from the data (‘hidden’). Using the data on length of family names (Figure 3), ‘Most family names had fewer than 7 letters’ is hidden in the data. Asking the question, ‘Do you think this would be the same in a different class?’ encourages students to consider moving beyond the data. Explicitly tying evidence to conclusions is a skill that needs practice and nurturing (Makar 2016).

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate: 

  • information
  • data
  • collect
  • category
  • display
  • symbol
  • list
  • table
  • column graph 
  • dot plot
  • vertical columns
  • horizontal bars
  • equal spacing
  • title
  • key
  • vertical axis
  • horizontal axis 
  • axes 
  • spreadsheet.

Collecting data

Creating effective survey questions often means trialling the questions and redrafting them to make them clearer. It is helpful to have a clear purpose for any survey. Keep the survey short and check that each question relates to the purpose.

The focus area of Data provides opportunities for teachers to incorporate contexts and topics from other key learning areas in mathematics. In Science and Technology students collect data from the tests and experiments they conduct. Mathematics outcomes in Data can be addressed in parallel with those in Science and Technology. Topics being studied in other key learning areas such as HSIE and PDHPE are also good sources of authentic data that can be used in mathematics lessons.

Equal interval scales

Equal interval scales have an equal separation between numbers (units) everywhere on the scale. For example, the separation between one and 2 must be the same as the separation between 29 and 30. The idea of an equal interval scale relates to the use of a scale for measuring length (Bell and Janvier 1981).

Many-to-one scales

A scale of many-to-one uses one unit or interval to represent more than one item or response, such as one centimetre representing 5 items or responses.

A dataset needs to contain a sufficiently large number of data points to warrant a many-to-one scale. A narrow range of values, such as one to 5, doesn’t need to use one. However, recording values that range from one to 83 would typically require a many-to-one scale.

Language

Matching statements on cards to graphs can model survey sentence structures and help students in using a specific set of vocabulary terms.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms to communicate: 

  • data
  • collect
  • survey
  • recording sheet
  • rating scale
  • category
  • display
  • symbol
  • tally mark
  • table
  • column graph
  • dot plot
  • vertical columns
  • horizontal bars
  • scale
  • equal spacing
  • title

  • vertical axis
  • horizontal axis
  • axes
  • spreadsheet
  • misleading.

Position

By convention when using grid-reference systems, such as those found on maps, the horizontal component of direction is named first, followed by the vertical component.

A grid reference locates a unique square region on a map rather than a single point. There are 2 parts to a grid reference:

  • the first letter or number tells you how far across the map something is
  • the second letter or number tells you how far up or down the map something is.

An Aboriginal Languages Map of Australia identifies Language Groups and the Nations to which they belong. It explains the relationship of a particular Aboriginal Nation and may identify significant landmarks or places on Country to which Aboriginal Peoples are connected. Using maps can support students in making connections to their local or known areas.

The grid-reference system is expanded on in Geography. In Mathematics, the grid-reference system is a precursor to introducing coordinates on the Cartesian plane in Stage 3, where the horizontal coordinate is recorded first, followed by the vertical coordinate.

Length

In Stage 2, measurement experiences enable students to develop an understanding of the size of the metre, centimetre and millimetre, to estimate and measure using these units, and to select the appropriate unit and measuring device.

Developing personal benchmarks to estimate

A benchmark is a standard against which something can be compared or measured. Students need to develop personal benchmarks with which to estimate lengths and other measures. Hand width, the unit used to measure the height of a horse, has developed from an informal unit to a standardised measure of approximately 10 cm.

Providing opportunities for students to find things in their environment that are 1 cm, 10 cm and 1 m can help establish benchmarks for convenient units of length. Direct experience of measurement units enables students to establish personal benchmarks and make reasonable estimates.

Students, including those with visual impairments (Jones et al. 2009), tend to be most accurate when estimating measurements ‘in the human scale’ and least accurate with very large or small estimates that cannot be directly experienced (Jones et al. 2009).

When recording measurements, a space should be left between the number and the abbreviated unit, eg 3 cm, not 3cm.

Angles

In Stage 2, students need informal experiences of creating, identifying and describing a range of angles. This will lead to an appreciation of the need for a formal unit to measure angles.

A simple 'angle tester' can be made by placing a pipe-cleaner inside a straw and bending the straw to form two arms. Another angle tester can be made by joining two narrow straight pieces of card with a split-pin to form the rotatable arms of an angle.

Two different coloured intersecting paper plates can be used to show angles as amounts of turn and for comparisons to quarter turns (Host et al. 2014).

Paper folding is a quick and simple means of generating a wide range of angles for comparison and copying.

Misconceptions with angles

The arms of the angles above are different lengths. However, the angles are the same size, as the amount of turning between the arms is the same. Students may mistakenly judge one angle to be greater in size than another based on the length of the arms of the angles in the diagram.

To assist students in understanding that the length of the arms does not affect the size of the angle, students should be exposed to angles in a variety of orientations and real-world situations. Students should also be exposed to angles where the arm lengths are different.

Language

Teachers can support students to use the language of mathematics by developing understanding that the same word can be used in a range of contexts. Some students may use ‘big’ to signify importance or ‘biggest’ to indicate intensity, such as those who use Aboriginal English. Making connections between concepts and ensuring that students know when the context is mathematical, can support students to select the most appropriate term to use.

Vocabulary

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms related to Position to communicate: 

  • position
  • location
  • map
  • plan
  • path
  • route
  • grid
  • grid reference
  • aerial view
  • directions.

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms related to Length to communicate: 

  • length
  • distance
  • metre
  • centimetre
  • millimetre
  • ruler
  • measure
  • estimate
  • handspan.

Students should be provided with opportunities to develop confidence in using some or all of the following terms related to Angles to communicate:

  • angle
  • amount of turning
  • arm
  • vertex
  • right angle.
